cosine build reads these files recursively, skipping folders that start with . and node_modules:
File | Read as
.md, .mdx, .markdown | Markdown. The page title comes from title in the front matter or the first # heading. MDX import/export lines and JSX tags are dropped. .html, .htm | The element (or , or ). Navigation, header, footer, scripts and elements with data-cosine-ignore are dropped. Pages with are skipped. .txt | Plain text.
URLs follow the file path: guides/cli.md with --base-url /docs becomes /docs/guides/cli, index.md becomes /docs/.

Every page is split at ##, ### and #### headings. Each section becomes one search result that links straight to the heading anchor (GitHub style, or a custom {#id}). Sections longer than --max-chars (default 1200) are split at paragraphs.
The model sees each chunk together with its page title and heading path, e.g. Billing > Invoices, so short sections still have context.

Option | Default |
--out | public/cosine | Output directory --base-url | / | URL prefix of the pages --model | english | english, multilingual or a Hugging Face model id, see Models --lexical-only | | No vectors, keyword search only --exclude | | Skip files whose relative path starts with this (repeatable) --max-chars | 1200 | Soft maximum chunk length --boost | | Rank results below a path higher (n above 1) or lower (below 1), repeatable, e.g. --boost /docs/api=1.5 --boost /blog=0.7 --synonyms | | JSON file with synonym groups, see Synonyms --incremental | | Reuse the vectors of the index in --out, embed only new and changed sections --shard-size | | Split the index into files of about n sections (whole pages stay together). The browser loads them in parallel and unchanged shards stay cached, see Large sites --vector-bits | 8 | 4 halves the vector file at a small cost in ranking quality

Keyword search only finds the words that are on the page. A synonym list helps with the words your visitors use instead, especially before the model has loaded or when it never loads:
{ "login": ["sign-in", "anmelden"], "invoice": ["bill", "receipt", "rechnung"] }
npx cosine build docs --synonyms synonyms.json
Every word in a group finds the others. A synonym ranks a little below the exact word. The list is stored in cosine-index.json, so the browser needs nothing else. An array of groups ([["login", "sign-in", "anmelden"]]) works too.

Not every page deserves the same rank. --boost weights a part of the site up or down. The weights are stored in the index:
npx cosine build docs --boost /docs/api=1.5 --boost /blog=0.7
Results below /docs/api rank 50 % higher, blog results 30 % lower. Paths match whole segments, the longest matching path wins, and a weight of 1 changes nothing. In code, boost works for buildIndex() (stored) and loadIndex() (override).

--incremental reads the index already in --out and embeds only sections whose text changed. A typo fix on one page then takes a second instead of embedding the whole site again. When the index was built with another model or passage prefix, or there is none yet, Cosine embeds everything and says so.
npx cosine build docs --out public/cosine --incremental # Reused 412 sections, embedded 3
Keep the output directory between CI runs (cache it like the model) to profit in CI too.

With thousands of pages cosine-index.json gets large. Two options keep it manageable:
cosine build docs --shard-size 2000 --vector-bits 4
--shard-size 2000 writes cosine-shard-0.json, cosine-shard-1.json and so on, plus a small cosine-index.json that lists them. The browser loads the files in parallel, and the result ranks exactly like one file. Unchanged shards keep their file name and content between builds when the pages before them did not change, so a CDN or the browser cache serves them again. Use it when a single file gets too big for your host or cache. --vector-bits 4 stores each vector value in 4 bits. The vector file is half the size, and in our tests the top ten of a query overlap in at least seven results with the 8-bit file. Check your own queries with a golden-queries test before you switch.
Format 2 also stores each page title and URL once instead of once per section, which made the index of these docs 15 percent smaller than format 1. The saving grows with many short sections.

Building downloads the model once (about 23 MB). Cache it between runs:
- uses: actions/cache@v4 with: path: node_modules/@huggingface/transformers/.cache key: cosine-model - run: npx cosine build docs --out public/cosine --base-url /docs
Cosine is a good target when you search documentation and want results by meaning, without a server. It is not a general search engine. Read the "Lose" column of each section before you switch.

Pagefind and Cosine have the same shape: both index your built site at build time and search in the browser without a server.
Pagefind | Cosine
npx pagefind --site dist | npx cosine build dist --out dist/cosine data-pagefind-body to pick the content | Cosine reads , then , then data-pagefind-ignore | data-cosine-ignore, or --exclude for whole files data-pagefind-weight, ranking per element | --boost /docs/api=1.5, ranking per URL path data-pagefind-filter and filter UI | facets attribute: filters by section of the URL, with counts. scope limits a search to paths Pagefind UI | pagefind.search(query) and result.data() | await cosine.search(query), results carry chunk, snippet and highlights Synonyms via custom configuration | --synonyms synonyms.json
What to change:
Replace the pagefind call in your build with cosine build, pointing at the built HTML or the Markdown sources. See Building the index. Replace the Pagefind UI script and stylesheet with the element, see Search field. Move data-pagefind-ignore attributes to data-cosine-ignore. Delete the pagefind output folder from your deploy.

You gain: results by meaning ("get rid of the app" finds "Uninstall"), hybrid ranking with exact words, typo tolerance before the model has loaded, section-level results with links to the heading, German, French and Italian texts.
You lose: Pagefind loads only the index parts a query needs, so it scales to very large sites. Cosine loads the whole index and, once the model is ready, compares against every vector. Beyond a few thousand pages, stay with Pagefind. Cosine has no filters on arbitrary metadata, only on URL paths. The model is a download of about 23 MB on first use (keyword results do not wait for it).

Orama | Cosine
create({ schema }) | No schema. A document is { id, url, title, content } insert / insertMultiple | buildIndex(documents), or cosine build Index lives in memory, optionally persisted | Index is two files (cosine-index.json, cosine-vectors.bin), written once at build time search(db, { term }) | cosine.search(term) mode: "fulltext" \ | "vector" \ | "hybrid" | mode: "lexical" \ | "semantic" \ | "hybrid" (default) Embeddings from your plugin or API | Built in with transformers.js, or your own Embedder (experimental, see Stability) facets on schema fields | cosine.facets(query) counts results per URL section where filters on fields | scope on URL paths only boost per field | --boost per URL path
What to change: build the documents once (from files with cosine build, or from a CMS with buildIndex), ship the two files, and load them with loadIndex. There is no insert at runtime.
You gain: nothing to design (no schema, no chunking code), sections with anchors out of the box, an accessible search field, incremental rebuilds.
You lose: arbitrary fields and filters, runtime inserts and updates, and control over the schema. If you search products or records instead of documentation, Orama is the better fit.

MiniSearch / Lunr | Cosine
new MiniSearch({ fields, storeFields }) / lunr(function () { this.field(...) }) | Not needed. Title, headings and text are indexed addAll(documents) / this.add(doc) | cosine build or buildIndex(documents) Serialised index (toJSON, lunr index JSON) | cosine-index.json plus the vector file search(q, { fuzzy: 0.2, prefix: true }) | On by default: close spellings match, and the last word matches as a prefix (instal finds install) search(q, { boost: { title: 2 } }) | Headings are indexed twice, so a heading match ranks higher. --boost ranks by URL path Lunr title:foo, +foo -bar, wildcards | "exact phrase" and -excluded words. No field queries or wildcards Your own result rendering | , or useCosine in React, or cosine.search() and your own markup
What to change: replace the index code with cosine build in your build step, replace the search call with await cosine.search(query), and render result.chunk.title, result.chunk.headings and result.snippet. Results are sections (not whole pages); pass groupByPage: true for one result per page.
You gain: semantic ranking, ready-made accessible UI, snippets with highlights, no hand-written index code.

You lose: field queries and wildcards, and a lot of size: MiniSearch and Lunr need no model. If you only need keyword search and want the smallest download, build with --lexical-only, which uses no model at all.
Cosine Pro converts an Algolia DocSearch export and its synonyms into a Cosine index. See Migrating from Algolia.

Search for five questions your visitors ask, in their words. Compare the first result with the old search. Add a synonym list for the words your product uses differently from your visitors. Check the size of public/cosine against Performance. Read the privacy notes: the model download is the only request to a third party, and you can host it yourself.

The index and the browser must use the same model. Cosine stores the model id in cosine-index.json and loads it automatically in the browser.
--model | Model | Size (q8) | Use when
english (default) | Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 | about 23 MB | Docs and queries in English multilingual | Xenova/multilingual-e5-small | about 120 MB | Docs in German, French or Italian, or queries in another language than the docs
Keyword search works in every language either way. Accents and ß are folded, so Grösse, Größe and grosse match.
German docs with the English model?

It works for words shared between the languages (product names, API names, technical terms), but semantic matches for German phrases are weaker. If most visitors search in German, use multilingual. Because the model loads only when the search field gets focus, the larger download does not slow down the page.

Any feature-extraction model with ONNX weights works. E5 and BGE models expect prefixes:
npx cosine build docs --model Xenova/bge-small-en-v1.5 --query-prefix "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: "

Semantic hits below a minimum cosine similarity are dropped so that nonsense queries find nothing. The English preset uses 0.2. Set your own when loading:
const cosine = await loadIndex("/cosine/cosine-index.json", { minSimilarity: 0.3 });

Queries: nothing. Search runs entirely on the visitor's device. There is no search API and no tracking. The index is loaded from your own site. The model is downloaded from huggingface.co the first time the search field gets focus, then served from the browser cache. This request reveals the visitor's IP address to Hugging Face, like any third-party asset.
If that request is a problem under the GDPR or the Swiss FADP for your site, serve the model yourself.
Serving the model from your own domain
or an index built with --lexical-only never contacts a third party.

Every recipe has the same two steps: build the index into a folder that the site serves as /cosine/, then add the search field. Install first:
npm i @sweberdev/cosine @huggingface/transformers
The index URL is always an absolute path such as /cosine/cosine-index.json. If your site lives below a base path, include it, see Troubleshooting.

Starlight sites work the same way. Add the integration. It indexes dist after astro build:
import cosine from "@sweberdev/cosine/astro";
export default defineConfig({ integrations: [cosine({ model: "english" })] });
The index lands in dist/cosine/. Without the integration, run cosine build dist --out dist/cosine after the build.
<cosine-search index="/cosine/cosine-index.json"></cosine-search>
<script> import "@sweberdev/cosine/element"; </script>
The Pro plugin cosine-vite builds the index inside the Astro build and serves it in dev.

Add the plugin. It indexes the built site after docusaurus build:
plugins: [["@sweberdev/cosine/docusaurus", { model: "english" }]],
The index lands in build/cosine/. Without the plugin, run cosine build build --out build/cosine after the build.
Swizzle the search bar and render the element on the client only:
import React from "react"; import BrowserOnly from "@docusaurus/BrowserOnly";
export default function SearchBar() { return ( <BrowserOnly> {() => { require("@sweberdev/cosine/element"); return <cosine-search index="/cosine/cosine-index.json" />; }} </BrowserOnly> ); }
During docusaurus start the index does not exist yet. Run cosine build build --out static/cosine once after a build to try the search in dev.

npx cosine build site --out site/cosine
<script type="module"> import "@sweberdev/cosine/element"; </script> <cosine-search index="/cosine/cosine-index.json"></cosine-search>
The bare specifier @sweberdev/cosine/element needs a bundler (Vite, esbuild, webpack) or an import map that points to a copy of the package you serve yourself.
Open the browser console first. Cosine logs errors there with the prefix cosine:.

Check these in order:
The build found your pages. cosine build prints Indexed 42 pages as 186 chunks. If the number is 0 or too low, check the directory you passed, the file extensions (.md, .mdx, .markdown, .html, .htm, .txt), your --exclude options, and whether HTML pages have (they are skipped). HTML pages have content in . Cosine reads , then , then . Elements with data-cosine-ignore are dropped. The index is found. Open /cosine/cosine-index.json in the browser. A 404 shows up in the console as cosine: could not load ... (404), and a missing index attribute as cosine-search: missing index attribute. No scope limits the search. A scope attribute or option hides everything outside those paths. The query is not only an exclusion. -retry alone has nothing to find. Add a word that should match. The semantic ranking does not cut your query. Semantic hits below the minimum similarity are dropped, so nonsense finds nothing. Try the same query with mode="lexical"; if that finds results, lower minSimilarity in loadIndex (see Models).
Try the query in the terminal: npx cosine search public/cosine "your query" --mode lexical.
Only keyword results, the model never loads

The status of the search is lexical until the model is requested, then loading-model and ready, or model-failed. Reasons for staying on keywords:
The browser asks to save data. With load-model="lazy" (the default), Cosine stays lexical when the visitor has "save data" turned on. Use load-model="eager" to load the model anyway. load-model="never", mode="lexical" or an index built with --lexical-only. These never load a model, on purpose. A Content Security Policy blocks the download. The model comes from huggingface.co, and transformers.js loads its WebAssembly runtime from a CDN. The console shows a CSP violation. Allow the hosts in connect-src, allow WebAssembly in script-src ('wasm-unsafe-eval') and, if needed, the CDN for scripts. Or serve both yourself, see Privacy and self-hosting, and the policy can stay strict. The visitor is offline or the host is blocked (a company firewall, a privacy extension). The status becomes model-failed and keyword search keeps working. @huggingface/transformers is not installed in the project that bundles the search.
The index files fail to load from another domain (CORS)

The browser fetches cosine-index.json and the vector file with fetch. From another origin (for example a CDN domain) the server must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin for your site. The simplest fix is to serve the index from the same domain as the page. If you use a CDN, add the header there, for both files.
Results link to the wrong page, or the index is not found

The index attribute is a URL as the browser sees it. If the site lives below /docs/, use index="/docs/cosine/cosine-index.json" and make sure the files are actually served there. Relative URLs depend on the current page, so prefer absolute paths. The links in the results come from the build: --base-url /docs makes guides/cli.md link to /docs/guides/cli. Set it to the path where the pages are served, or the clicks end in 404 pages. With a framework that adds a trailingSlash or .html suffix, check one result URL in the console (cosine-results event) against the real page URL. If they differ, build from the generated HTML instead of the sources, since Cosine maps about/index.html to /about/. Use cosine-select with preventDefault() to navigate with your router when the site is a single page application, see Search field.

Check the size of public/cosine first, and compare it with Performance: the vectors need about 390 bytes per section, the manifest also contains the text of every section.
Exclude pages nobody searches: --exclude drafts/, --exclude changelog/. Raise --max-chars to get fewer, longer sections (the default is 1200). Build with --lexical-only when you do not need the model: no vector file, no model download. Serve the files compressed (gzip or Brotli). The JSON compresses very well. If the site has tens of thousands of pages, Cosine is the wrong tool, see Why Cosine.
"the index has N chunks but M vectors" or "built with X, the embedder uses Y"

Both errors mean that cosine-index.json and the vector file do not belong together, or the model does not match the vectors.
Different builds. A CDN or the browser cache served an old vector file next to a new manifest (or the other way round). Deploy both files together and purge the cache for both. Different model. The index stores the model id. A custom embedder must use the same model as the one the index was built with. Rebuild with the model you want to use at search time. Different prefixes. For E5 and BGE models, build and search with the same --query-prefix and --passage-prefix, they are stored in the index. When in doubt, rebuild: npx cosine build docs --out public/cosine (without --incremental).
The filter buttons do not show

The facets attribute (or prop) must be set on . With a single section in the results there is nothing to filter, so the buttons stay hidden. Search for a word that appears in more than one section. Filters are per section of the URL path. If all your pages share the first path segment (/docs/...), use facets="2" to filter by the first two (/docs/guides, /docs/api). Custom CSS can hide them. They are exposed as ::part(facets).
Changes to the pages do not show up in search

The index is built at build time. Run cosine build again before you deploy, and make sure the build runs after the site is generated if you index built HTML. A browser may hold an old cosine-index.json in its cache; a hard reload fixes it, and your host's cache headers decide how long it lasts for visitors.
Open an issue at github.com/Weber-Development/cosine with the console output, the output of cosine build and the version of @sweberdev/cosine.

<script type="module"> import "@sweberdev/cosine/element"; </script>
<cosine-search index="/cosine/cosine-index.json" lang="de" shortcut="mod+k"></cosine-search>
It works in any framework or none: Astro, VitePress, Docusaurus, Hugo, Eleventy, plain HTML.

Attribute | Default |
index | | URL of cosine-index.json, or several separated by spaces to search them as one, see Several indexes lang | page language | en, de, fr or it for the built-in texts placeholder, label | from lang | Custom texts limit | 8 | Number of results shortcut | / | /, mod+k (Ctrl K / ⌘K) or none mode | hybrid | lexical never loads the model load-model | lazy | lazy (on focus), eager (right away), never facets | off | Shows filter buttons per section of the site with the number of results. facets="2" uses two path segments (/docs/guides) scope | whole index | Space-separated URL paths to search in, e.g. /docs/api /docs/guides
scope matches whole path segments: /docs/api covers /docs/api/auth, but not /docs/apis. Use it for a search field that only covers one section, such as the API reference.

Visitors can narrow a search without any setup:
Query | Finds
"reset password" | Sections that contain these words next to each other, in this order webhook -retry | Sections about webhooks that do not contain retry sign-in, e-mail | Normal words: only a - at the start of a word excludes
Phrases and exclusions apply in every mode, also to the results of the semantic ranking. Small words such as the do not break a phrase. Accents and case are ignored, like everywhere else.

Add the facets attribute and the dropdown shows a button per section of the site (docs (7), blog (3)), plus All. A click limits the results to that section. With a single section there is nothing to filter, so the buttons stay hidden. Style them with ::part(facets).
<cosine-search index="/cosine/cosine-index.json" facets></cosine-search>
For your own search page, use the API:
cosine.facets(query) counts the results per section of the site, so your own search page can offer filters and use the chosen path as scope:
const facets = await cosine.facets("webhook", { depth: 2 }); // [{ path: "/docs/guides", count: 7 }, { path: "/docs/api", count: 3 }] const results = await cosine.search("webhook", { scope: facets[0].path });

One site, several sources: the docs, the blog, a help center. Build an index for each and list them in index; Cosine searches them as one and merges the results by rank.
<cosine-search index="/docs/cosine-index.json /blog/cosine-index.json" facets></cosine-search>
In code, loadIndexes(urls, { weights }) returns a CosineGroup with the same search, searchLexical, facets, warmup and onStatus as Cosine. weights ranks an index higher, e.g. { weights: [2, 1] } puts the docs first. Every index must be built with the same model, which cosine build does by default. Each result has an index field with the position of its index.

The field follows the ARIA combobox pattern: arrow keys move through the results, Enter opens one, Esc closes the list and then clears the field. The number of results is announced to screen readers, matches are marked with , and animations respect reduced motion.
Each result is a link with role="option", so there is no link nested inside an option. The filter buttons are real buttons with aria-pressed. Every release is tested in Chromium with Playwright (keyboard, ARIA attributes, narrow screens, reduced motion) and scanned with axe-core against WCAG 2.1 AA, with the list open and the filters shown. The tests are in packages/e2e in the repository.

cosine-select fires before navigating, with the SearchResult as detail. Call preventDefault() to navigate yourself, e.g. with a client-side router:
document.querySelector("cosine-search").addEventListener("cosine-select", (event) => { event.preventDefault(); router.push(event.detail.chunk.url); });

Most documentation search either needs a hosted service (Algolia DocSearch, Typesense, a vector database) or matches only exact words (Pagefind, Lunr, FlexSearch). Someone who types "how do I get rid of the app" finds nothing on a page titled "Uninstall".
Cosine closes that gap without a server:

Index at build time. cosine build splits your Markdown, MDX or built HTML into sections and stores a small vector for each section next to your site, e.g. in public/cosine/. Search in the browser. The visitor's browser compares the query with these vectors (cosine similarity, hence the name). The model runs locally through transformers.js. Instant first, smart second. Keyword results show up on the first keystroke. The model (about 23 MB, cached by the browser) loads in the background when the search field gets focus, and the ranking improves as soon as it is ready. Visitors with "save data" turned on keep keyword search. Typo-tolerant. A word that is not in the index also finds close spellings, so instalation still finds the installation guide, even before the model has loaded. Synonyms. A synonym list in the index lets login find the page that says sign in. Fast rebuilds. cosine build --incremental embeds only the sections that changed. Hybrid ranking. Keyword and semantic results are combined with reciprocal rank fusion, so exact API names still win where they should. Accessible search field.
is an ARIA combobox that works with keyboard and screen readers, in English, German, French and Italian. React hooks are available too.

| Size
Library (search + web component) | about 7 KB gzip Index for 100 pages (about 400 sections) | about 160 KB vectors + the text Model, English (default) | about 23 MB, loaded once, then from the browser cache Model, multilingual | about 120 MB, recommended only when queries and pages use different languages
Queries never leave the browser. The only outside request is the model download, from Hugging Face by default, or from your own server. See Privacy and self-hosting.
Tens of thousands of pages: the index then gets too big for the browser. Use a search server. Search across content that changes every minute: Cosine indexes at build time.

@weber-development/cosine-answers reads the top results of a search, picks the sentence that best answers the question and shows it with a link to the page. It runs in the browser, needs no account or API key and gives the same answer every time.
npm i @weber-development/cosine-answers
Add it to the search element
attachAnswer returns a function that removes the listener again.

You get null when confidence is below minConfidence, when fewer than half of the question's words are covered, or when two different pages answer about equally well. Nothing is better than a wrong answer.
The answer is extractive: it quotes your docs and never rewrites them. If no page states the answer in one or two sentences, there is none. Only the top three results are read.
renderAnswer escapes all text and only links relative, http and https URLs. Style it with .cosine-answer, .cosine-answer-text and .cosine-answer-link.

The question and the sentences are compared after a light stemmer folds plurals and common endings, so "settings" matches "setting". Set the language of your docs with lang: en, de, fr, es, it, nl or pt. The default auto picks the language by counting common words in the question and in the top results, and falls back to English.
attachAnswer(searchElement, answerElement, { lang: "de" });

@weber-development/cosine-astro is the ready-made plugin for Astro and Starlight. It builds the index in astro dev and astro build, swaps Starlight's search for , and uses one index and model per language on multilingual sites.
pnpm add @weber-development/cosine-astro @sweberdev/cosine

With two or more Starlight locales (or Astro i18n.locales in plain Astro) every language gets its own index in dist/cosine/ /. English uses the small English model, other languages the multilingual one, and a visitor downloads only the model of the language they read. Choose the models yourself with models:
cosineStarlight({ models: { en: "english", de: "multilingual", fr: false } })
See Languages for how a page's language is detected.

Option | Default |
docs | src/content/docs | Folder with the pages baseUrl | Astro base | URL prefix of the pages models | | Model per language model | english | One model for the whole site, or false for keyword search only cacheFile | node_modules/.cache/cosine/embeddings.json | Embedding cache, or false shardSize | | Split the index into files of about this many sections keepPagefind | false | Starlight plugin only: keep Pagefind as well
The other options (exclude, maxChars, code, vectorBits, ...) are those of the Vite plugin.

Tested with Astro 7.3 and Starlight 0.42; older Astro versions are not tested. Only content below docs is indexed, not pages written as .astro files. Cosine's field replaces Starlight's modal dialog; on narrow screens it shares the header with the site title. Verified with real astro build and astro dev runs and the generated HTML. Not verified in a real browser.

@weber-development/cosine-docusaurus is a ready-made plugin and theme for Docusaurus 3. It renders in the navbar search item and builds the search index of every locale after docusaurus build. The free @sweberdev/cosine/docusaurus integration only indexes; this package adds the search box, the embedding cache and models per locale.
pnpm add @weber-development/cosine-docusaurus @sweberdev/cosine @huggingface/transformers

Option | Default | Meaning
model | english | Model for locales without an entry in models; false for keyword search only models | | Model per locale, e.g. { en: "english", de: "multilingual" } out | cosine | Folder of the index in the built site cacheDir | node_modules/.cache/cosine | Embedding cache; false turns it off exclude | | Paths of the built site to skip. 404.html and assets/ are always skipped shardSize | one file | Split the index into files of about this many sections synonyms | | Groups of words that mean the same boost | | Weight per path vectorBits | 8 | 4 or 8

Docusaurus builds each locale on its own, so each locale gets its own index, built with the model you chose for it. The search box loads the index of the locale the visitor is reading and uses the locale's language for its texts. The default locale's index does not contain the pages of other locales.
Embeddings are cached per locale and model in node_modules/.cache/cosine. A rebuild embeds only sections that changed. Cache that folder in CI.

Colours come from the Docusaurus variables (--ifm-color-primary, --ifm-background-color, --ifm-font-color-base and others), so dark mode follows the theme. For more control, style cosine-search::part(input) and ::part(panel) or swizzle SearchBar.

No index in the dev server; build first. Page titles are the HTML , usually Page | Site name. The search box shows in the desktop navbar only, like the classic search item. The mobile menu has none. With a model, webpack bundles the Hugging Face runtime (about 27 MB of WebAssembly in the output). Browsers load it only when search is first used. Tested with a real docusaurus build of Docusaurus 3.10 (classic preset, two locales) and checked in the generated HTML and bundle. Not tried in a real browser.

@weber-development/cosine-i18n is for sites in several languages. The English model is about 23 MB, the multilingual one about 120 MB. With one index for everything, every visitor downloads the large model. With one index per language, English pages use the small model, German and French pages use the multilingual one, and a visitor downloads only the model of the language they are reading.
npm i -D @weber-development/cosine-i18n

<cosine-search></cosine-search> <script type="module"> import "@sweberdev/cosine/element"; import { mountLanguageSearch } from "@weber-development/cosine-i18n/client"; mountLanguageSearch(document.querySelector("cosine-search"), "/cosine/cosine-languages.json"); </script>
mountLanguageSearch reads . It picks the exact language (pt-BR), then the base language (de for de-CH), then the default, and sets index and lang on the element. Pass a language as the third argument to override . loadLanguageIndex and languageIndexUrl return the URL if you build the field yourself.
How a page gets its language

In this order:
lang: (or language:, locale:) in the front matter a language suffix in the file name: intro.de.md a language folder in the file id or the URL: de/intro.md, /de/intro your own detect function (detectLanguage in the Vite plugin), which runs before these three rules otherwise the default language: defaultLanguage, by default the first one
Only the languages you list can match, so a folder called deploy is not read as German.

A language can be keyword-only (de: false), use another Hugging Face model (de: " ") or bring its own embedder and synonyms: de: { embedder, synonyms: [["Rechnung", "Faktura"]] }. Shared synonyms, boost, chunking options and shardSize apply to every language.

The presets are the two that ship with Cosine, english and multilingual. Other models work through their Hugging Face id, but they are untested. A visitor reading a language that has no index gets the default language's index. Queries cannot search across languages in one field. For that, use one multilingual index or give the field several indexes (index="/cosine/en/cosine-index.json /cosine/de/cosine-index.json"), which loads both models.
Every search that finds nothing is a page someone wanted and you have not written. @weber-development/cosine-insights collects those searches and turns them into a to-do list.

npx cosine-insights report --log data/searches.ndjson --out insights.html --since 2026-09-01
The report lists:
Searches without results: missing pages, or missing words in existing ones. Results nobody opened: the search found something, but it did not look like the answer. Most searched queries and most opened pages, the click rate and the mean rank of opened results.
--out insights.md writes Markdown, e.g. for a monthly issue. --out insights.csv (or --format csv) writes the query lists as one table for a spreadsheet or your ticket system, with the columns list (no-results, no-clicks, top), query, searches, clicks and results. From code: analyze(events), renderMarkdown(report), renderHtml(report), renderCsv(report).

npx cosine-insights trends --log searches.ndjson --out trends.html
trends compares the last 28 days (--days changes the length) with the 28 days before:
New gaps: queries that found nothing in the last period and were not a problem before. These are the pages to write next. Resolved gaps: queries that found nothing before and now find something or get opened. This is the proof that your fixes work. Rising: queries searched clearly more often than before. By week: searches, searches without results and clicks per week, as a chart in the HTML report.
--out trends.md writes Markdown for a monthly issue, --out trends.csv the weekly series (week,searches,no_results,clicks). The log needs timestamps, which the handler adds. From code: analyzeTrends(events, { days }), renderTrendsHtml(trends), renderTrendsMarkdown(trends), renderTrendsCsv(trends).
Find out why a query failed

npx cosine-insights suggest --log searches.ndjson --index public/cosine --out gaps.md
For every query without results, suggest checks the index and says which of three cases it is:
Probably a typo: a word is not in your docs, but a similar one is. The report shows the corrected query and the page it finds. Use it to fix a link or add the word as a synonym. Closest pages: the words are known, but no page covers them together. The report lists the pages that come closest. Nothing comes close: no page covers the topic. This is the list of pages to write.
--semantic also looks pages up by meaning, which needs an index with vectors and @huggingface/transformers. --limit, --min and --since work as in report. From code, use the suggest entry, which needs @sweberdev/cosine:
import { suggestFixes, renderSuggestionsMarkdown } from "@weber-development/cosine-insights/suggest";

This GitHub Action runs every Monday, reads the log, and opens an issue with the trends and the gaps. Keep the log where your job can reach it, for example in a private storage bucket, and give the job its address as a secret.

name: Search report on: schedule: - cron: "0 6 * * 1" workflow_dispatch: permissions: contents: read issues: write jobs: report: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 - name: Install run: | echo "@weber-development:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com" >> .npmrc echo "//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${{ secrets.COSINE_PRO_TOKEN }}" >> .npmrc npm i --no-save @sweberdev/cosine @weber-development/cosine-insights - name: Fetch the log run: curl -fsSL "${{ secrets.SEARCH_LOG_URL }}" -o searches.ndjson - name: Build the report run: | npx cosine-insights trends --log searches.ndjson --days 7 --out trends.md npx cosine-insights suggest --log searches.ndjson --index public/cosine --since "$(date -d '7 days ago' +%F)" --out gaps.md cat trends.md gaps.md > report.md - name: Open an issue env: GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }} run: gh issue create --title "Search report $(date +%F)" --body-file report.md

COSINEPROTOKEN is the read-only token from the install guide. The workflow needs your built index in public/cosine; if you build it in CI instead, add that step before the report. Without a server log, point SEARCHLOGURL at wherever your handler's store writes.

npx cosine-insights dashboard --log data/searches.ndjson --index public/cosine --out dashboard.html
The dashboard is a single HTML file with no external requests: overview numbers, the gaps with suggested fixes, weekly trends, the most searched content and CSV downloads for each table. Open it locally or put it behind your login. --semantic also uses the embedding model for the fix suggestions.

People often search for a word your docs never use: "reimbursement" where the page says "refunds". The search finds nothing, the visitor leaves. cosine-insights synonyms turns those searches into synonym groups you can review and feed back into the index.
npx cosine-insights synonyms \ --log data/searches.ndjson \ --index public/cosine \ --existing synonyms.json \ --out synonyms.suggested.json \ --md proposal.md \ --semantic

It takes the queries that found nothing or that nobody clicked. A word of those queries is a candidate when it appears in no section of your index and was searched at least --min-count times (default 2). With --semantic, it takes the top hit of the semantic search for the word. From the title and headings of that section, the word or short phrase that is most similar to the candidate becomes the other half of the group. Candidates below a similarity of 0.45 are listed as "No fit found". Without --semantic no groups are proposed.
A word that is one or two edits from a known word is a typo, not a synonym. Typos are listed in the proposal in their own table and are never added to a group.

--out receives your existing groups unchanged, followed by the new ones, without duplicates. The format is an array of arrays, the same as cosine build --synonyms:
[ ["login", "sign-in"], ["refunds", "reimbursement"] ]
--md receives the proposal: every suggested group with how often it was searched, the queries and the top page, then the typos and the words without a fit. Review it before you merge: a group is only right when both words mean the same in your docs.

The package contains a ready-made GitHub Actions workflow, examples/synonyms-pr.yml. It runs every Monday, writes synonyms.json and opens a pull request on the branch cosine/synonyms with the proposal as its description. Only synonyms.json is committed. You merge it, the next build uses the groups.
Option | Meaning
--log | The NDJSON log of the insights handler --index | The folder with cosine-index.json --existing | Your synonyms.json; a missing file counts as empty --out | Merged groups as JSON (default synonyms.suggested.json) --md | The proposal as Markdown --min-count | Searches a word needs (default 2) --semantic | Look for synonyms by meaning; needs vectors in the index and @huggingface/transformers --since | Only searches from this date

Events go to your own server, never to us or a third party. No IP address, cookie, user id or header is stored, only query, result count, opened URL, rank and time. Queries that look like e-mail addresses, phone or account numbers, IBANs or tokens are dropped in the browser and again on the server.
Mention the search statistics in your privacy notice all the same.

In the Algolia dashboard open your index and use Manage index → Export, or browse the index with the API. Cosine reads a JSON array, an object with a hits array, or NDJSON. Synonyms come from Configuration → Synonyms.

DocSearch stores one record per heading or paragraph. The tool groups them by page URL, then:
hierarchy.lvl1 becomes the page title. lvl2 and deeper become ## to #### headings, with the anchor from the URL hash, so results link to the exact section. Content records become the text under their heading, in the order of weight.position. Flat hierarchy_lvl0 keys work like the nested form.
URLs are reduced to path and hash, so the same index works on staging and production. --keep-origin keeps the domain.

Algolia | Cosine
synonym (several words that mean the same) | one synonym group oneWaySynonym | one group of the input and its synonyms placeholder, altCorrection | dropped
The command prints how many groups were converted and how many were dropped.

Option | Default |
--records | | Export from Algolia. Required --synonyms | | Synonyms export --out | public/cosine | Output directory --keep-origin | off | Keep the domain in URLs --lang | all | Only records of this language --model | english | english, multilingual or a Hugging Face model id --lexical-only | off | No embeddings, keyword search only --incremental | off | Reuse the vectors of the index already in --out --boost | | Rank results below a path higher or lower, repeatable

Algolia's ranking rules and facets are not copied. Use boost for sections that should rank higher, and facets on the search element to filter by path. Once the new search works, remove the DocSearch script and delete the Algolia index.

After output: "export": the out/ folder. Otherwise: the prerendered pages in .next/server/app and .next/server/pages. These exist for every static page and every page with generateStaticParams. Pages that only render on request have no HTML at build time and are not indexed.
Next's error pages (404, 500, _not-found) are skipped, and so are pages with . Like the free CLI, Cosine reads the element, so navigation and footers stay out of the results. Mark other elements with data-cosine-ignore.
The index is written to public/cosine, which Next serves from /cosine/. Use --base-path when your site has a basePath.

The last index is kept in .next/cache/cosine. The next build embeds only sections whose text changed and takes the rest from there. Vercel and most CI setups keep .next/cache between builds, so a typo fix does not embed the whole site again. --no-cache embeds everything.

Cosine Pro adds what you need once search runs on more than one site: the index builds itself, and you see what people look for and do not find.
Package | What it does

@weber-development/cosine-vite | Builds the index in every Vite build (Astro, VitePress, SvelteKit, Nuxt), serves it in dev, rebuilds on change and re-embeds only the sections that changed @weber-development/cosine-next | Builds the index from the pages next build has prerendered and keeps the last index in .

next/cache, so CI rebuilds embed only what changed @weber-development/cosine-migrate | Turns an Algolia DocSearch export and its synonyms into a Cosine index @weber-development/cosine-insights | Records searches without tracking people and reports queries without results, results nobody opened, the most searched topics and how they change from period to period @weber-development/cosine-answers | Quotes the sentence that answers the question above the results, with a link to the page, without an LLM @weber-development/cosine-quality | Golden queries: write down which page must answer which search and let CI fail when a change makes search worse @weber-development/cosine-i18n | One index per page language, each with its own model: English pages use the small model, other languages the multilingual one, and visitors download only the model of the language they read @weber-development/cosine-docusaurus | Docusaurus plugin and search bar theme: the index per locale, with cache and shards @weber-development/cosine-vitepress | VitePress config wrapper and theme that puts the search field in the nav bar @weber-development/cosine-astro | Astro integration and Starlight plugin that replaces the built-in search
Plans and prices are on packages.sweber.dev/cosine. After cancelling a subscription, the versions you installed keep working; only updates and access to new versions end.

@weber-development/cosine-quality checks your search against golden queries: a list of queries with the page that should come up. It reports the hit rate and the mean reciprocal rank (MRR), and it fails when a query that worked before stops working. Keyword search is enough, so the check needs no model and no network and gives the same result every time.
pnpm add -D @weber-development/cosine-quality

[ { "query": "install", "expect": "/docs/getting-started" }, { "query": "timeout", "expect": ["/docs/configuration", "/docs/network"], "within": 5 }, { "query": "log in", "expect": "/docs/auth", "within": 1, "mode": "hybrid" } ]
Field | Meaning
query | What a visitor types. Each query appears once expect | A URL path prefix, or an array of them. Any hit counts. /docs/api matches /docs/api/auth, not /docs/api-keys within | The expected page must be among the first within pages. Default 3 mode | lexical or hybrid. Default lexical; with --semantic the default is hybrid
Start with 20 to 50 queries: the ones your visitors search most (see cosine-insights report) and the ones that were once broken.

npx cosine-quality check --index public/cosine --golden golden.json
The output is a short summary. Add --out report.md for a Markdown report with the failing queries and what was found instead.

Write the current state once and commit it:
npx cosine-quality check --index public/cosine --golden golden.json --write-baseline
From then on, compare every run with it:
npx cosine-quality check --index public/cosine --golden golden.json \ --baseline quality-baseline.json --min-hit-rate 0.9
The command exits with 1 when
a query that passed in the baseline fails now, the mean rank of the shared queries got worse, or the hit rate is below --min-hit-rate.
It exits with 2 when a file cannot be read or the golden file is invalid; the message names the entry. After a change you intended, write the baseline again.

--semantic loads the embedding model and ranks like the search box does (hybrid). It needs an index with vectors and @huggingface/transformers, and it is slower. Queries with "mode": "lexical" stay keyword-only.

name: Search quality on: pull_request
jobs: quality: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 cache: pnpm - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile env: COSINE_PRO_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.COSINE_PRO_TOKEN }} - run: pnpm build - name: Check search quality run: | set +e npx cosine-quality check --index public/cosine --golden golden.json \ --baseline quality-baseline.json --min-hit-rate 0.9 --out quality-report.md code=$? cat quality-report.md >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY" exit $code
The report shows on the summary page of the run, and a regression fails the check.

Build: writes cosine/cosine-index.json and cosine/cosine-vectors.bin into the output folder. In tools that run a server and a client build (Astro, SvelteKit) the files go to the client build. Dev: serves the index from memory and rebuilds it when a file in docs changes. The browser receives the Vite event cosine:update. Cache: vectors are stored in node_modules/.cache/cosine/embeddings.json by section text. A rebuild after editing one page embeds only that page's changed sections. Cache that folder in CI to make builds fast.

import cosine from "@weber-development/cosine-vite"; export default defineConfig({ vite: { plugins: [cosine({ docs: "src/content/docs", baseUrl: "/" })] } });
import cosine from "@weber-development/cosine-vite"; export default defineConfig({ vite: { plugins: [cosine({ docs: ".", baseUrl: "/", exclude: ["node_modules", ".vitepress"] })] } });

Option | Default |
docs | | Folder with the pages, relative to the Vite root baseUrl | / | URL prefix of the pages model | english | english, multilingual, a model id, or false for keyword search only embedder | | Custom embedder instead of model outDir | cosine | Folder of the index below the site base cacheFile | node_modules/.cache/cosine/embeddings.json | Embedding cache, or false exclude | | Paths below docs to skip maxChars, code, minLevel, maxLevel | | Chunking, as in Building the index languages, defaultLanguage, detectLanguage | | One index per page language with its own model, see Languages shardSize, vectorBits | | Split the index into shards of about this many sections, and 4-bit vectors, see Large sites
cachedEmbedder(embedder, file) is exported too, for your own build scripts.

@weber-development/cosine-vitepress puts where the built-in VitePress search normally sits and builds the index as part of vitepress dev and vitepress build. It works with VitePress 1.x and its locales.
pnpm add -D @weber-development/cosine-vitepress @sweberdev/cosine @huggingface/transformers

Option | Default | Meaning
model | english | Model of a site without locales, or false for keyword search models | | Model per locale key, e.g. { root: "english", de: "multilingual" } exclude | node_modules, public | Folders below srcDir that are not docs shardSize, outDir, cacheFile, synonyms, ... | | As in the Vite plugin ui | | placeholder, shortcut (mod+k), facets, limit, mode, loadModel
The colours come from the --vp-c-* variables, so the field follows light and dark mode.

Tested with VitePress 1.6.4 in real builds and a dev server, not in a real browser. srcExclude is not read, use exclude. The index is built from the Markdown source, not from the rendered page. VitePress 2 (alpha) is not supported.

Loads cosine-index.json and the vector file next to it and returns a Cosine instance.
Option | Default |
loadModel | lazy | lazy loads the model on warmup() or the first search (not when the browser asks to save data), eager right away, never not at all embedder | from the index | Your own Embedder, or false for keyword search only minSimilarity | from the index | Drop semantic hits below this cosine similarity boost | from the index | Ranking weights per URL path, e.g. { "/docs/api": 1.5 }, replacing the ones stored in the index synonyms | from the index | Synonym groups, e.g. [["login", "sign-in"]], replacing the ones stored in the index fetch | globalThis.fetch | Custom fetch

Member |
search(query, options?) | Promise . mode: hybrid (default; keyword results until the model is ready, does not wait), lexical, semantic (waits for the model). limit (8), groupByPage (false), scope (URL paths to search in, a string or an array) facets(query, options?) | Promise : the results of a query counted per section of the site, most first, e.g. /docs/guides 12, /docs/api 5. depth (path segments per facet, default 1), limit (results counted, 200), plus mode and scope. Use a path as scope to search only there searchLexical(query, options?) | Synchronous keyword search warmup() | Loads the model. Never rejects; on failure status becomes model-failed status | lexical, loading-model, ready, model-failed onStatus(listener) | Subscribe to status changes, returns an unsubscribe function chunks | All chunks of the index

loadIndexes(urls, options?) loads several indexes and returns a CosineGroup; new CosineGroup(members, { weights }) groups indexes you loaded yourself. It has search, searchLexical, facets, warmup, status, onStatus and chunks like Cosine, merges results by rank, and adds index (position of the index) to each result. weights ranks an index higher. See Several indexes.

interface SearchResult { chunk: { id: number; doc: string; url: string; title: string; headings: string[]; text: string }; score: number; matchedBy: Array<"lexical" | "semantic">; snippet: string; highlights: Array<[start: number, end: number]>; // ranges in snippet }
highlightParts(snippet, highlights) splits a snippet into { text, match } parts for rendering.

Function |
buildIndex(documents, options) | Chunks and embeds { id, url, title, content } documents. Returns { manifest, vectors, reused, embedded }. synonyms stores synonym groups in the index, boost stores ranking weights per path, previous ({ manifest, vectors } of the last build) reuses the vectors of unchanged sections transformersEmbedder(options) | Embedder on top of transformers.js. model (english, multilingual or an id), dtype (q8), device, queryPrefix, passagePrefix, load, onProgress chunkMarkdown(document, options) | Splits one Markdown page into chunks htmlToMarkdown(html) | Extracts the main content of an HTML page
From @sweberdev/cosine/node: readDocs(dir, options), writeIndex(index, outDir, { shardSize }), buildDirectory(dir, outDir, options), readIndex(dir) (the last build, for previous), loadIndexFile(path, options).

Anything with this shape works, e.g. a call to your own embedding API at build time:
interface Embedder { model: string; embed(texts: string[], kind: "query" | "passage"): Promise<Float32Array[]>; }
Reading and writing the index yourself

parseManifest(json) turns the content of a cosine-index.json (format 1 or 2) into a manifest with all sections. serializeManifest(manifest) writes the compact format 2. indexFiles(builtIndex, { shardSize }) returns the files of an index as { name, data } (the manifest, the vector files and, with shardSize, the shards), for build tools that emit files themselves. See Migrating to 2.0.
cosine build <docs-dir> [options]     Build a search index from Markdown, MDX and HTML files cosine search <index-dir> <query>     Try a query against a built index

Option | Default |
--out | public/cosine | Output directory --base-url | / | URL prefix of the pages --model | english | english, multilingual or a Hugging Face model id --lexical-only | | No embeddings, keyword search only (no model download) --exclude | | Skip files whose path starts with this (repeatable) --max-chars | 1200 | Soft maximum chunk length --query-prefix | | Prefix for queries (custom E5/BGE models) --passage-prefix | | Prefix for passages (custom E5/BGE models) --boost | | Rank results below a path higher (n above 1) or lower (below 1), repeatable, e.g. --boost /docs/api=1.5 --boost /blog=0.7 --synonyms | | JSON file with synonym groups, see Building the index --incremental | | Reuse the vectors of the index in --out, embed only new and changed sections --shard-size | | Split the index into files of about n sections (whole pages stay together). The browser loads them in parallel and unchanged shards stay cached, see Large sites --vector-bits | 8 | 4 halves the vector file at a small cost in ranking quality
Writes cosine-index.json (format 2: chunks and settings) and cosine-vectors.bin (int8 vectors, or 4-bit with --vector-bits 4) to the output directory.

Option | Default |
--mode | hybrid | hybrid, lexical or semantic --limit | 5 | Number of results
Exit code 0 on success, 1 on errors.

Most sites upgrade by installing 2.0 and rebuilding the index. This page lists every breaking change, so you can check whether it touches you.
npm i @sweberdev/cosine@latest @sweberdev/cosine-react@latest npx cosine build docs --out public/cosine   # same command as before, now writes format 2
If you use Cosine Pro, update to 1.0.1 or later of the Pro packages first. They accept Cosine 2.x. Pro 2.0 is not required: Pro 1.x works with Cosine 2.
@sweberdev/cosine needs Node 22 for the CLI, @sweberdev/cosine/node and the build integrations. Node 20 reached its end of life in April 2026. The browser code has no new requirement.

cosine build now writes version: 2. The file is smaller (15 percent for these docs): page id, URL and title are stored once per page, and every section is a short array instead of an object. Cosine 2 still reads format 1, with one console.warn; Cosine 1.x cannot read format 2. Rebuild when you upgrade, and deploy the new index together with the new JavaScript.
Do you read cosine-index.json yourself? Then your code sees arrays where it saw objects. Use the parser instead of JSON.parse:
import { parseManifest } from "@sweberdev/cosine";
const manifest = parseManifest(await (await fetch("/cosine/cosine-index.json")).json()); manifest.chunks[0].url; // as before
loadIndex, loadIndexes, loadIndexFile and readIndex already do this.
Words in Chinese, Japanese, Thai and similar scripts

These scripts have no spaces between words. Cosine 1 treated a whole run of characters as one word. Cosine 2 splits them with Intl.Segmenter, so a search for 東京 finds 東京タワー and the snippet highlights it. The side effect is that results for these languages change. Nothing is stored in the index for this, so a rebuild is not needed.
Accent folding now only applies to Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic and Hebrew text. Before, it also stripped marks in other scripts, for instance the dakuten that tells か from が.
Embedder, transformersEmbedder and DEFAULT_MODEL lose their @experimental tag. This changes no behaviour. The presets in MODELS stay experimental.

The default model stays english (23 MB). A multilingual default would make every English site download about 120 MB. Pick --model multilingual if your pages or visitors are not English. Everything marked deprecated in 1.x: nothing was deprecated, so nothing is removed. The web component, its attributes, parts and events, and the React components.

Compact index, shards and 4-bit vectors for large sites: Large sites. Integrations @sweberdev/cosine/astro (Starlight too), /docusaurus and /vitepress: Recipes. Words and highlighting for languages without spaces. Browser tests in Firefox and WebKit next to Chromium on every pull request. Cosine Pro: golden-query tests (cosine-quality), synonym proposals as a pull request, answers in more languages. See Cosine Pro.
Security and bug fixes for 1.x continue for 12 months after the day 2.0.0 is released.

The numbers on this page come from packages/core/test/bench.test.ts. The test builds a synthetic site of 1000 pages (3000 sections of about 60 words each) and measures the result. It runs on every pull request with fixed limits, so a change that makes the index or the search several times worse fails the build.

Measured with npx vitest run test/bench.test.ts --disableConsoleIntercept on a Linux virtual machine with 4 cores, which is about what a CI runner offers. One run, so expect some variation between runs and machines.
What | Measured | Limit in CI
Keyword search over 3000 sections, median | 1.0 ms | 5 ms Keyword search over 3000 sections, 95th percentile | 1.6 ms | 20 ms Build of 3000 sections without embeddings | 193 ms | 3000 ms Manifest overhead per section (title, url, headings, without the text) | 169 bytes | 400 bytes Vectors per section (384 dimensions, 8 bit) | 388 bytes | 400 bytes
The limits sit a few times above the measurements on purpose. They catch real regressions, not a slow runner.
What it means for your site

The index is the text of your pages plus about 170 bytes per section for the manifest and about 390 bytes per section for the vectors of the default model. Both compress well when your host serves gzip or Brotli.
Site | Sections | Vectors | Manifest overhead
100 pages | about 400 | about 150 KB | about 70 KB 1000 pages | about 3000 | about 1.1 MB | about 500 KB
The text of the pages comes on top of that. The table assumes 3 sections per page, as in the benchmark. Real pages differ, so check the count in the cosine build output.
What the benchmark does not measure

Embedding time. cosine build with a model takes seconds to minutes depending on the number of sections and the machine. --incremental embeds only changed sections. Model download and start. The English model is about 23 MB (multilingual about 120 MB). It loads once, when the search field gets focus, and comes from the browser cache afterwards. Keyword results do not wait for it. Semantic search time. After the model is ready, each query is embedded in the browser and compared with all vectors. This depends on the device and is not part of the CI limits. Real network and slow phones. The numbers above are for desktop-class CPUs.
For the limits of the approach, see Why Cosine.
From 1.0 on, Cosine follows semantic versioning. Version 2.0 is the second major release: it changes the index format and removes what 1.x had marked for removal. See Migrating to 2.0.

Patch releases (1.0.x) fix bugs. They do not change documented behaviour. Minor releases (1.x.0) may add exports, options, attributes, parts and events, and optional fields to the index. They do not remove or rename anything in the frozen list below. Major releases (2.0) are the only place for breaking changes.
An index built with any 1.x version loads in every 1.x version of the browser code. Newer versions may add optional fields that older code ignores, so a feature that needs a new field (like synonyms did) works only after you rebuild the index.
Everything below keeps its name, its signature and its documented behaviour in 1.x.

loadIndex(url, options?), loadIndexes(urls, options?) and the class CosineGroup. The class Cosine with search, searchLexical, facets, warmup, status, onStatus and chunks. The status values lexical, loading-model, ready and model-failed. SearchOptions (limit, mode with hybrid, lexical and semantic, groupByPage, scope) and the shape of SearchResult. The options of loadIndex: loadModel, embedder, minSimilarity, synonyms, boost, fetch. The query syntax: "exact phrases" and -excluded words.

buildIndex from @sweberdev/cosine, and buildDirectory, readIndex, writeIndex, readDocs and loadIndexFile from @sweberdev/cosine/node. The options of buildIndex: embedder, synonyms, boost, previous, maxChars, vectorsFile and onProgress, plus baseUrl and exclude for buildDirectory.

The commands cosine build and cosine search . The options --out, --base-url, --model, --lexical-only, --exclude, --max-chars, --query-prefix, --passage-prefix, --synonyms, --boost, --incremental, --mode, --limit and --help.

The element and its attributes index, lang, placeholder, label, limit, shortcut, mode, load-model, scope and facets. The parts field, input, shortcut, panel, facets, results, result, result-title, result-snippet and status. The events cosine-results and cosine-select, with their detail fields. The custom properties --cosine-accent, --cosine-bg, --cosine-text, --cosine-muted, --cosine-border, --cosine-radius, --cosine-max-height and --cosine-z. In @sweberdev/cosine-react: CosineSearch, useCosine and useCosineSearch.

cosine-index.json with version: 2. 2.x writes version 2 and reads versions 1 and 2 (version 1 prints one warning). New fields are always optional, so older code ignores them. A new required field would be a new version, and that needs a major release. The root manifest of a sharded index (shards) and the shard files it lists. The vector file next to the manifest, named in manifest.vectors.

These parts work and are tested, but they may change in a minor release. They are marked @experimental in the type definitions.
The model presets in MODELS. The model ids behind the keys can change in a minor release, because they follow what runs well in transformers.js. The keys english and multilingual stay. Chunking rules. How a page is split into sections (heading levels, --max-chars, what is dropped from MDX and HTML) can improve in a minor release. Section ids and anchors may change as a result, so rebuild the index when you upgrade.
Embedder, transformersEmbedder and DEFAULT_MODEL are stable from 2.0: the Embedder interface may get new optional members, and a custom embedder written for 2.0 keeps working.
The helpers that @sweberdev/cosine also exports (chunkMarkdown, htmlToMarkdown, parseFrontMatter, slugify, tokenize, normalize, makeSnippet, fuse, LexicalIndex, VectorStore and similar) exist so you can build your own UI or pipeline. Their names are frozen too, but their exact output follows the experimental rules above where it depends on chunking or tokenizing.

When something has to go:
A minor release marks it as deprecated in the documentation and the type definitions (@deprecated) and, where the call is a function, prints one console.warn per page load or process that names the replacement. It keeps working for the whole minor series that follows, and for the rest of the 1.x line unless it has a security problem. It is removed in the next major release, and the upgrade notes say what to do.
Nothing is deprecated today. Index format 1 is read with a warning in 2.x and is removed in 3.0.

packages/core/test/api-surface.test.ts lists the runtime exports of @sweberdev/cosine, @sweberdev/cosine/node and @sweberdev/cosine/element, the methods of Cosine and CosineGroup, the attributes and parts of and the options in the CLI help text. The lists are written out literally, and the test runs in CI on every pull request.
If you remove or rename something, the test fails. Adding an export fails the test as well, so a new name is always a conscious decision: add it to the list in the same pull request. Within 1.x, only additions to the lists are allowed.

2.0 is a major release. It needs Node 22, writes index format 2 and changes how scripts without spaces are split. Read Migrating to 2.0; most sites only update and rebuild. See Stability for what 2.x promises.
Every version before it was also additive, with one exception: 0.8 changed the markup of the results list (see below). @sweberdev/cosine and @sweberdev/cosine-react are released together with the same version number. Index files stay at format version 1 throughout, but an index built with an older version lacks newer features, such as synonyms or boost weights, until you rebuild it.
Version | What is new | What to do

Self-hosted changelog and "What's new" widget, built from your Changesets, CHANGELOG.md, commits, GitHub or GitLab Releases. No SaaS, no tracking.
Derivative turns the changelog you already keep into a "What's new" button for your app. It reads Changesets output, any CHANGELOG.md in the Keep a Changelog or conventional-changelog style, conventional commits with version tags, or GitHub and GitLab Releases, and writes a static changelog.json, an Atom feed and a changelog page.
The widget is a single web component of about 6 kB gzipped with an unread badge, keyboard and screen reader support, dark mode and labels in English, German, French and Italian. The feed ships with your app and the read state stays in the browser, so there is no third-party service, no cookie and nothing to add to your privacy policy. A lean alternative to hosted tools such as Beamer or Headway.

Reads Changesets (default and GitHub formats), Keep a Changelog, conventional-changelog, conventional commits with tags, GitHub Releases and GitLab Releases (self-managed too); monorepo feeds can be limited to chosen packages; Linear cycles, Jira versions and Notion pages as sources (beta) derivative build writes changelog.

json, an Atom feed, a JSON Feed and a standalone changelog page; derivative init sets it all up in one step : popover or inline, unread badge, optional search field, about 6 kB gzipped, no dependencies Highlights shown as a toast, banner or modal for the newest release, once per reader; major releases come first, the modal traps focus and closes with Escape Accessible: labelled dialog, focus handling, Escape to close, reduced motion respected, a correct heading outline, and axe and real-Chromium checks (contrast, RTL, phone width) in the test suite Labels and dates in English, German, French and Italian; dark mode, right-to-left pages, a dozen CSS custom properties and styleable parts Release communication: a title, summary, images or video, call-to-action links and an importance per release; translations inside the feed; entries and releases for chosen audiences; "new" hints on your own UI elements A frozen API with a written stability promise, deprecation policy, migration guide and upgrade guide, checked by tests and by installing the packed release into example projects; feed format 2 is a superset, version 1 feeds are still read Bindings for React ( , useChangelog, an unstyled ) and Vue 3 ( , useChangelog); Svelte, Astro and plain HTML use the element directly
Read statistics without cookies or visitor IDs: opens, reads and link clicks per release, plus a "Was this helpful?

" vote under each release, with an HTML report, a password-protected dashboard route for your own backend, CSV export and storage in a file, Postgres or SQLite; emoji reactions and comments under each release, stored in your own database, plain text and approved by you before they show Audience segments and languages: entries only for certain plans or roles, scheduled releases, feature-flag audiences (Unleash, LaunchDarkly), translations written into the feed with DeepL, an OpenAI-compatible model or Anthropic, and a cache so only changed texts cost anything Release notes with approval: drafts as JSON files in your repository (draft, review, approved, publish date), a CI check, and optional AI-written first drafts with your own key that always need a person's approval; import from Linear, Jira and Notion as drafts, with all pages read and retries on rate limits (beta) Announcements: a subscriber list with double opt-in and e-mail digests sent through Resend, Postmark, Amazon SES or any SMTP server (one-click unsubscribe, consent evidence), plus posts to Slack, Teams, Discord, Mattermost, Google Chat, Mastodon, Bluesky and LinkedIn

Counts opens, reads and link clicks per release on your own endpoint, adds a helpful / not helpful vote under each release, without cookies or visitor IDs, and renders a report or serves a dashboard route. Readers can also react with an emoji and leave comments on a release, which you moderate.

Shows entries only to the plans or roles they are meant for, publishes releases on a schedule, translates the feed into more languages (inside the feed or one file per language) with DeepL, an OpenAI-compatible model or Anthropic, and manages drafts with an approval step, including AI-written first drafts. Entries can follow your Unleash or LaunchDarkly feature flags Imports releases from Linear, Jira and Notion as drafts (beta).

Keeps a subscriber list with double opt-in, sends new releases, with image and links, as an e-mail digest in the reader's language through Resend, Postmark, Amazon SES or your own SMTP server, and posts them to Slack, Teams, Discord, Mattermost, Google Chat, Mastodon, Bluesky and LinkedIn.
Does Derivative send data to a server?
No. The feed is a static file you deploy with your app, and the widget stores the last release a reader has seen in their browser's local storage. Nothing else is stored or sent.
I don't use Changesets. Does it still work?
Yes. Derivative also reads Keep a Changelog and conventional-changelog files, or builds the feed from conventional commits and version tags. You can also write changelog.json by hand or from a CMS.
Can I write friendlier release notes than my commit messages?

Yes. Highlights in derivative.config.json add a title, a summary, images, links and an importance to any release, while the generated entries stay as they are. With Pro you can also keep drafts in your repository and have them approved before they are published.

Yes. The widget is a standard web component, so it works in plain HTML and in any framework. There are ready-made bindings for React and Vue 3, and Svelte and Astro need no wrapper (the docs show how).
Can I use the open-source part on its own?
Yes. @sweberdev/derivative and @sweberdev/derivative-react are MIT-licensed and complete without Pro. Pro adds statistics, segments and announcements on top of the same changelog.json.
I use Derivative 1.x. What changes with 2.0?

The feed format grows to version 2 and the widget's announce attribute becomes highlight; version 1 feeds are still read, and the CLI can write the old format with --feed-format 1. Node 22 is required. The migration guide in the documentation lists every change. Version 1.x keeps getting fixes for 12 months.
Do readers need an account to comment?

No. With Derivative Pro, readers can react with an emoji and leave a comment without an account. Comments are plain text, stored in your own database, held back until you approve them and never sent to us. You are responsible for them as personal data, so mention them in your privacy notice.

Install the package:
pnpm add @sweberdev/derivative
With npm: npm i @sweberdev/derivative.
Set it up in one step:
npx derivative init
init looks at the project, writes derivative.config.json (source and output files) and puts derivative build in front of your build script, so the feed is rebuilt with every deploy. It never overwrites an existing config; pass --no-scripts to leave package.json alone. To do the same by hand, read on.
Build the feed. With a CHANGELOG.md in the project root (for example from Changesets):
npx derivative build
Without a changelog file, Derivative reads your git history instead. It needs version tags (v1.2.0) and conventional commits (feat:, fix:):
npx derivative build --source git
Both write public/changelog.json. Add the build to your build script so the feed is always current:
{ "scripts": { "build": "derivative build && vite build" } }
Add the widget where the button should appear, for example in your header:
<derivative-widget src="/changelog.json" lang="de"></derivative-widget> <script type="module"> import "@sweberdev/derivative/widget"; </script>
In React, use the React component instead.
Open the app. The button shows how many releases are new, and opening it marks them as seen.
Node.js 22 or newer for the CLI git on the PATH for --source git and for release dates of Changesets changelogs Any current browser for the widget (custom elements and shadow DOM)

Run derivative build before your app build so the feed ships with each deploy:
{ "scripts": { "build": "derivative build --atom public/changelog.xml && next build" } }
For --source git and for dates of Changesets releases, the build needs the tags. Many CI systems clone shallowly without them. On GitHub Actions:
- uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: fetch-depth: 0 # full history and tags
On Vercel, git history is not available during the build. Commit the generated public/changelog.json instead, for example in the Changesets version PR:
{ "scripts": { "version": "changeset version && derivative build" } }
Add the Atom feed to your page head so readers can subscribe:
<link rel="alternate" type="application/atom+xml" title="Changelog" href="/changelog.xml" />

Four small projects in the examples folder show the widget in a real framework. Each one reads its own CHANGELOG.md, writes public/changelog.json (or static/ in SvelteKit) before the build, and embeds the widget with announce and search.
Folder | Framework | How the widget is added
vite | Vite | web component, imported in src/main.ts nextjs | Next.js 15, App Router | WhatsNew from @sweberdev/derivative-react in app/layout.tsx sveltekit | SvelteKit, Svelte 5 | web component, imported in onMount astro | Astro 5 | web component, imported in a page
Copy a folder, run pnpm install and pnpm dev. The examples are built against the published package on every change, so they keep working. For details see the guides for React, Vue and Svelte.

Generated entries are precise but dry. For releases that deserve attention, add a highlight in derivative.config.json. It is merged into the generated release by version:
{ "highlights": { "2.4.0": { "title": "Dark mode is here", "summary": "Switch it on under **Settings → Appearance**.", "importance": "major", "media": [{ "type": "image", "url": "/changelog/dark-mode.png", "alt": "The dashboard in dark mode" }], "links": [{ "label": "Read the guide", "url": "https://acme.ch/docs/dark-mode" }], "audience": ["beta"] } } }
Field | Meaning
title, summary | Shown instead of the version (which moves next to the date) and above the entries importance | major makes the widget's highlight prefer this release over newer minor ones media | Images and videos (type: "image" or "video"), shown above the entries. Give images an alt text; decorative ones get an empty one links | Calls to action under the entries and in the modal audience | Only readers with a matching audience attribute see the release
The widget, the HTML page, the Atom feed and the JSON Feed use them. In format 1, a single image field did the job of media; it is still read.

Derivative 2.0 turns the widget from a list of changes into a way to talk to readers: a richer feed format, a modal and a banner for the releases that matter, audiences, translations and hints inside your product, and read-only sources for Linear, Jira and Notion. The Pro packages add an approval workflow and drafts. Most installations need one search-and-replace.
1.x keeps getting security and bug fixes for 12 months after 2.0.0.

Node.js 22 or newer for the CLI, the node entry point and the Pro packages (Node 20 reached its end of life). The widget in the browser is not affected. Update all packages together: @sweberdev/derivative, -react and -vue (and the three Pro packages) to 2. Rename the announce attribute to highlight (React and Vue: the announce prop to highlight). The derivative-announce event is now derivative-highlight, and dismissToast() is dismissHighlight(). If you style the toast with ::part(), rename toast to highlight, toast-title to highlight-title, toast-action to highlight-action and toast-dismiss to highlight-dismiss. The CSS custom properties stay the same. Replace image by media in your highlights and hand-written feeds (see below). If you read changelog.json yourself, expect "version": 2. Run derivative build, open the page and click through the widget.

1.x | 2.0
| (a toast, as before). highlight="banner" and highlight="modal" are new Event derivative-announce | derivative-highlight dismissToast() | dismissHighlight() Parts toast, toast-title, toast-action, toast-dismiss | highlight, highlight-title, highlight-action, highlight-dismiss Release field image: "/a.png" | media: [{ "type": "image", "url": "/a.png", "alt": "…" }]. A feed with image is still read and converted Highlights accept title, summary, image | They accept title, summary, media, links, importance and audience. image is no longer part of the type; an image in a config file is still read and converted Feed.version: 1, createFeed writes 1 | Feed.version: 2. createFeed writes 2 ({ format: 1 } for 1) parseFeed returns the feed as written | It returns format 2 for both formats Node.js 20 | Node.js 22
