import { swipeRows } from "@weber-development/lagrangian-pro"; const rows = swipeRows(list, { onChange: (row, open) => {} }); The first child of a row slides to the left and reveals the [data-actions] behind it. Place the actions at the right edge of the row, under the content. A flick opens or closes the row, the content rubber-bands at the ends, a vertical drag still scrolls the page, and only one row is open at a time (single: false changes that). The buttons are not reachable with Tab while the row is closed. With the keyboard, Alt+ArrowLeft opens the focused row, Escape or Alt+ArrowRight closes it. rows.open(row), rows.close() and rows.isOpen(row) are there for code.

Texts and visuals are yours: the functions set no colours, sizes or labels beyond what the behaviour needs. lightbox and formSheet mark their state with attributes (aria-expanded on the thumbnail, data-state on the sheet) that you can style.

From Lagrangian Pro 2.1 the form sheet, the gallery and swipeable rows are available as one function each. The examples below show how to build such patterns from the parts yourself.
All examples use the framework-free API. In React, use the hook with the same name and put ref directly on the element.
A form in a bottom sheet

On release the sheet projects where the throw would come to rest with friction and picks the nearest detent, so a short flick moves it as far as a long drag. Past the highest detent it rubber-bands. Without a handle, dragging starts anywhere on the sheet unless the pointer is in scrolled content.

import { useSheet } from "@weber-development/lagrangian-pro-react";
const sheet = useSheet({ detents: [0.4, 1], backdrop: backdropRef }); <button onClick={() => sheet.open()}>Filters</button> <div ref={sheet.ref} className="sheet" data-open={sheet.index >= 0} />

import { flip, measure } from "@weber-development/lagrangian-pro";
flip(grid, () => grid.prepend(card));            // children of grid spring into place
const snapshot = measure(grid);                   // before a framework update // … DOM changes … snapshot.play({ duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 });    // before the next paint
Elements that are already moving keep their velocity when a second change arrives.

Hold an item near the edge of the window or of a scrollable parent and the list scrolls by itself, faster the closer you get to the edge. The dragged item stays under the pointer and the slot is recomputed while the page moves. autoScroll: { edge: 56, speed: 900 } tunes it (pixels and pixels per second), autoScroll: false turns it off.

editor.value;        // the spring as an options object editor.code();       // "{ duration: 0.45, bounce: 0.12 }" editor.set({ stiffness: 300, damping: 20 }); editor.setMode("physical"); await editor.play(); editor.destroy();

Every element has a class that starts with spring-editor-: -modes, -mode, -curve (an SVG that draws in currentColor), -stage, -ball, -play, -row, -label, -input, -value, -stats, -code, -copy. The ball and the stage have a small inline size so the editor works without any CSS. Pass messages to translate the texts, for example `{ play: "Abspielen", copy: "Code kopieren" }`.

Give an element on both pages the same data-shared value. On push the element of the new page starts where the old one is, with its size, and springs to its own place. On pop it flies back to where the page below shows it.
Shared elements fly on push and on pop(). A swipe back follows the finger and does not fly them. Use another attribute with the shared option.

A self-hosted audit log for SaaS apps: who changed what, and when. Field-level diffs in your own Postgres or SQLite, and a ready React view for your customers' admins.
Sooner or later a B2B customer asks who changed what in their account, and security questionnaires, ISO 27001 and SOC 2 audits ask the same. Logarithm records it with one call: actor, action, targets and a field-level diff computed from the state before and after. Passwords, tokens and card numbers are never stored, also inside nested objects.
Events live in your own database: Postgres 13+ (also Neon and Supabase), MySQL 8 and MariaDB, or SQLite (better-sqlite3, node:sqlite, Bun). Every event belongs to a tenant, and a scoped log cannot read other tenants. A Fetch API handler serves Next.js, Remix, Hono or Workers, and the React view shows your customers' admins an activity log with search, filters, day groups and diffs, in English, German, French and Italian. No external service, MIT-licensed.
