Component | Behaviour
ConsentGate | Renders children only with consent, otherwise fallback. ConsentScript | Injects an external script once consent exists. Renders nothing. ConsentIframe | Shows a placeholder with Load once and Always allow until consent exists.
Each takes either category or service. A service follows its category unless the visitor changed that service individually.
<ConsentScript category="statistics" src="https://example.com/analytics.js" allowlist={["https://example.com/"]} onError={(e) => console.warn(e)} />
Load once shows the embed without storing anything. Always allow stores consent for that single service, with source embed.

For scripts that come from a CMS or a tag snippet, mark them as inert and enable blockedElements on the provider (or call activateBlockedElements(manager) from the core):
<script type="text/plain" data-consent-category="statistics" data-consent-src="https://example.com/analytics.js"></script>
<script type="text/plain" data-consent-service="hotjar"> /* inline code runs after consent */ </script>
<iframe data-consent-category="marketing" data-consent-src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID" title="Video"></iframe>
Activated scripts keep all other attributes. Use data-consent-type="module" for module scripts.
allowlist accepts URL prefixes or regular expressions. Scripts outside the list are not loaded, even with consent. This protects against injected markup.

Code that already ran cannot be unloaded by any consent tool. After consent_revoked, reload the page if a script must stop:
manager.on("consent_revoked", () => window.location.reload());

Permito makes no network requests of its own and evaluates no strings, so it works under a strict policy such as default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'. Three things need your attention.

By default the script tag build and createConsentUI insert the default stylesheet as a element. A style-src without 'unsafe-inline' blocks that (Chromium logs "Refused to apply inline style"). Choose one of:
Link the stylesheet yourself and turn the injection off:
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/permito/styles.css" /> <script type="application/json" id="permito-config"> { "config": { "consentVersion": "2026-10", "categories": [] }, "injectStyles": false } </script>
styles.css is at @permitojs/core/styles.css. The React package imports the same file, so bundlers emit it as a normal stylesheet and nothing is inlined.
Or keep the injection and give the element your nonce with "styleNonce": " " in the config (or the styleNonce option of createConsentUI), and allow that nonce in style-src.
Permito sets document.body.style.overflow while a dialog is open. That goes through the CSSOM, which a CSP does not block.

ConsentScript, loadScript and activateBlockedElements create elements after consent. Under script-src with a nonce, pass the nonce:
loadScript({ src: "https://example.com/tag.js", nonce }); activateBlockedElements(manager, { nonce });
If you do not pass one, activateBlockedElements copies the nonce of the blocked element, so putting your nonce in the markup is enough. Third-party hosts you load after consent must be allowed in script-src (or reached through 'strict-dynamic') and connect-src; Permito cannot know them.
The Consent Mode default snippet is an inline script. Render it with your nonce:
<script nonce={nonce} dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: getConsentModeDefaultScript() }} />
The configuration for the script tag build sits in . That is a data block, not executable, so it needs no nonce.
Subresource Integrity for the script tag build

When you load permito.global.js from a CDN, pin the version and add the hash of the file:
curl -s https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@permitojs/core@0.7.0/dist/permito.global.js \ | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary | openssl base64 -A
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@permitojs/core@0.7.0/dist/permito.global.js" integrity="sha384-<hash from above>" crossorigin="anonymous" data-config="#permito-config" ></script>
Never use an unpinned URL together with integrity, because the next release would no longer match. Hosting the file on your own origin avoids the CDN and lets script-src 'self' apply. Update the hash with every upgrade.

Consent Mode needs two parts.
A default before any Google tag. Everything is denied except security_storage:
import { getConsentModeDefaultScript } from "@permitojs/react/server";
<script dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: getConsentModeDefaultScript() }} />
Updates after a decision. Enable googleConsentMode on the provider, or call connectGoogleConsentMode(manager) from the core. Permito then pushes gtag("consent", "update", …) whenever the decision changes.

Google consent type | Permito categories (all must be granted)
adstorage, aduserdata, adpersonalization | marketing analytics_storage | statistics functionalitystorage, personalizationstorage | preferences security_storage | necessary
Override it with googleConsentMode={{ mapping: { analytics_storage: ["statistics"] } }}. The same mapping must be passed to getConsentModeDefaultScript({ mapping }).
Permito is not a Google-certified CMP and does not implement IAB TCF. Publishers serving Google ads (AdSense, Ad Manager) in the EEA, UK or Switzerland may need a certified CMP. Check Google's current requirements.

A decision made in one tab applies immediately in every other open tab of the same site, including gated scripts, iframes and Google Consent Mode updates. Permito uses a BroadcastChannel and sends nothing over the network. Decisions for another consentVersion are ignored.
It is on by default with the built-in cookie storage. With your own storage (for example memory storage in a demo) turn it on with syncTabs: true; turn it off with syncTabs: false. Without React, call manager.destroy() when you throw a manager away.

Available since 0.4.0. Besides Google Consent Mode, three common tools have their own consent API. Permito forwards the decision to each of them, on load when a decision is stored and on every change. Which category a tool belongs to stays your decision; the defaults below are only a starting point.
Tool | Option | Default categories | Signal
Microsoft UET (Microsoft Advertising) | microsoftUet | marketing | uetq.push("consent", "update", { ad_storage }) Microsoft Clarity | clarity | statistics (analytics), marketing (ads) | clarity("consentv2", { analyticsStorage, adStorage }) Matomo | matomo | statistics | _paq.push(["setConsentGiven"]) or ["forgetConsentGiven"]

<PermitoProvider config={config} microsoftUet clarity matomo>
UET and Matomo also need a default before their tags run, so they wait for consent. Render it in :
import { getMatomoDefaultScript, getMicrosoftUetDefaultScript } from "@permitojs/react/server";
<script dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: getMicrosoftUetDefaultScript() + getMatomoDefaultScript() }} />
Clarity needs no default: without a granted signal it runs without cookies (check your Clarity project settings).

{ "config": { "consentVersion": "2026-10", "categories": [ … ] }, "microsoftUet": true, "clarity": true, "matomo": true }
The script-tag build pushes the UET and Matomo defaults itself as soon as it runs. Load permito.global.js in without defer, before the UET and Matomo snippets.

microsoftUet: { categories: ["marketing"], queueName: "uetq" } clarity: { analytics: ["statistics"], ads: ["marketing"] } matomo: { categories: ["statistics"], mode: "tracking" } // or "cookies"
With Matomo mode: "cookies", Matomo tracks without cookies until consent (requireCookieConsent, setCookieConsentGiven). Whether cookieless tracking without consent is allowed for your site is your assessment. Permito keeps the decision itself, so Matomo receives the non-persistent commands on every page view and stores no consent cookie of its own.
These APIs belong to Microsoft and Matomo and can change. Check their current documentation before go-live.

Permito 2.0 adds purposes and a webhook for withdrawal across systems, and changes the stored decision to make that possible. Most sites change nothing but the version number. Visitors keep their decision.

Purposes next to categories, see Configuration. connectConsentWebhook and parseConsentWebhookPayload, see Withdrawal across systems. hasPurposeConsent, setPurposeConsent, and the hooks and stores useHasPurposeConsent (React, Vue) and purposeStore (Svelte). Node 22 or later is required for building and for server-side use (Node 20 is end of life).
Change | Who is affected | What to do

The stored decision is schema 2 and has a purposes field. | Code that reads or writes the decision itself: custom ConsentStorage, code that builds a ConsentState by hand, test fixtures. | A custom storage can keep get() returning what it stored: schema 1 and schema 2 are both accepted and a schema 1 decision is upgraded when loaded. set() now receives schema 2. Type old fixtures as ConsentStateV1. ConsentSnapshot has a required purposes field. | Code that builds or mocks a snapshot. | Add purposes. ConsentManager has two new members (hasPurposeConsent, setPurposeConsent). | Code that implements or mocks the manager. | Add them. The events consentupdated and consentrevoked carry origin, consent_revoked also purposes. | Only code that builds events by hand. Listeners keep working. | None. readConsentFromCookieHeader, parseConsentState and isConsentState can return or accept a schema 1 decision. | TypeScript code that assumed ConsentState, for example a prop typed initialState: ConsentState \ | null that receives the cookie. | Type it ConsentState \ | ConsentStateV1 \ | null (both are exported by @permitojs/core and @permitojs/react), or call migrateConsentState.
Runtime behavior is unchanged. Node 22+ | Builds and servers on Node 20. | Upgrade Node.

All category based APIs (hasConsent, update, the components, hooks, stores and the script tag) behave as in 1.x. The built-in banner and preference center still work per category. A decision stored by 1.x is read and upgraded in place: every purpose follows its category, so a visitor who allowed marketing has all marketing purposes allowed. Nobody is asked again, and consentVersion does not need to change. Without purposes in your config, each category is one purpose with the category's id.
One thing to know about downgrading

A decision saved by 2.0 is schema 2, which 1.x does not read. If you roll back to 1.x, visitors who decided after the upgrade see the banner again. Visitors who decided before the upgrade keep their decision as long as nobody changed it.

pnpm add @permitojs/core@^2 @permitojs/react@^2
Pin both to the same version, they are released together. Before the final release you can try the release candidates with @next.

Permito Pro 1.0.1 and later accept Permito 2.x as peer, so upgrade Pro first (it works with both). Pro packages do not read the stored decision directly. Pro 2.0 adds the webhook receiver and the connectors, see the Pro documentation.
1.x gets bug and security fixes for 12 months from the release of 2.0.0, see Versioning and support.

There are no breaking changes between 0.1.0 and 1.0.0. Version 1.0.0 has the same code as 0.9.0; it adds the stability promise. Every release added to the API, and the stored decision format (schema 1) has not changed, so visitors keep their choice when you upgrade. Three behavior details are worth knowing.
Since | Detail | What to check
0.2.0 | With the built-in cookie storage, a decision now syncs across open tabs (syncTabs, default on). | If you create managers dynamically, call manager.destroy() when you drop one. Set syncTabs: false to turn it off. 0.3.0 | The stylesheet lives in @permitojs/core/styles.css. | @permitojs/react/styles.css still works. No change needed. 0.5.0 | es, nl, pl and pt are built in. | A site that used these language codes with its own translations keeps its texts, because overrides win. Without overrides the built-in texts apply now instead of English.

1.0.0 freezes the API listed as stable on the API status page. The runtime exports of every entry point are pinned by a test, so a change cannot slip in unnoticed. To upgrade:
Upgrade Permito Pro first if you use it (0.8.0 or later accepts Permito 1.x), then @permitojs/core and @permitojs/react. Pin both to the same version. They are released together. Run your own accessibility check against your theme and texts, see Accessibility.
Breaking changes only come with a new major version, with a migration note here. A deprecated API stays for at least one minor release and is marked @deprecated in the types.
Permito Pro 0.8.0 and later accept Permito 0.1 up to, but not including, 2.0 as a peer. Older Pro versions stop at 1.0.0: upgrade Pro first, then Permito.

If you use a nonce-based CSP, pass the nonce to the inline Consent Mode script and to ConsentScript (nonce prop) or to blockedElements={{ nonce }}.
A complete, tested example lives in examples/nextjs.

A consent banner stops scripts in the browser. When a visitor withdraws consent, that is only half of the job: the newsletter tool, the CRM and the analytics backend still hold the data and keep processing it unless something tells them to stop. The GDPR expects withdrawal to be as easy as giving consent and to take effect. India's DPDP Act (section 6) additionally requires that processors stop once consent is withdrawn.
Permito covers the browser. This guide shows how the withdrawal gets to your servers, and how to test that it reached every system.
This is technical infrastructure, not legal advice. Which systems you must update and how fast is a decision for you and your counsel.

Side | What happens | Tool
Browser | Scripts stop loading, blocked embeds go back to placeholders, Consent Mode updates, other tabs follow. | Permito core, nothing to add. Server | Your backend learns that consent changed and tells every system that holds data for the affected purposes. | connectConsentWebhook plus a receiver you build (or Permito Pro).

Give each processing purpose a stable id that you also use in the backend:
const manager = createConsentManager({ consentVersion: "2026-10", categories: [{ id: "necessary", required: true }, { id: "marketing" }], purposes: [ { id: "newsletter", category: "marketing" }, { id: "ad-personalisation", category: "marketing" }, ], services: [ { id: "mailtool", name: "Mail tool", category: "marketing", purposes: ["newsletter"] }, ], });
Send every change to your server
Send every change to your server

event is consentupdated or consentreset (the visitor deleted the decision). revoked lists exactly what this change withdrew. Without a subject, the payload contains no personal data and your backend cannot tell whose consent changed, so pass one if you want to act on a specific person. Adding it is your decision as the operator.

Idempotence. Retries repeat the id. Store it and ignore repeats. Authentication. The browser cannot hold a secret. Treat the endpoint as public: rate-limit it, validate the payload, and only act for a subject you can verify (a signed session, not the value in the payload alone). Own failures. If a downstream system is down, keep the withdrawal in a queue and retry. A withdrawal that was received but not applied is the case an auditor asks about. Offline visitors. A browser that is offline when the visitor withdraws cannot send. The decision is still stored in the browser, the webhook follows on the next change. If you need a guarantee, also compare the stored decision on the server side at login.
Permito Pro adds a ready-made receiver that writes into the consent log (with seals) and applies withdrawals to connected systems, see the Pro documentation.

Run this whenever you add a system or change a purpose:
Consent to all purposes in a fresh browser profile. Check that each system has the visitor's data (or the flag that allows processing). Withdraw one purpose in the preferences. Check that the webhook arrived (revoked.purposes has that purpose) and that exactly the systems for that purpose stopped. Systems for the other purposes keep working. Withdraw everything and then delete the decision (manager.reset()). Check the consent_reset event and that every system stopped. Consent again. Check that processing resumes only for the purposes granted. Stop your receiver, withdraw, start it again. Check that the withdrawal is applied after the retry and that a duplicate delivery changes nothing.
Keep the result of this test with your records. It is the evidence that withdrawal works across systems, not only in the browser.

The DPDP Act is a different law with different duties and definitions, and Permito does not map its text. The technical mechanism is the same: consent per purpose, withdrawal that is propagated and provable. If you need Hindi or other Indian languages for the banner, you can supply them through translations today; they are not built in.
Available since 0.3.0. The script-tag build renders the same banner and preference center as @permitojs/react, with the same texts, translations and styles, and needs no bundler.

Download permito.global.js from the @permitojs/core package (folder dist/) and upload it to your own server, e.g. /assets/permito.global.js. Self-hosting keeps the promise that Permito makes no third-party requests.
If you prefer a CDN, pin the version:
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@permitojs/core@0.3.0/dist/permito.global.js" data-config="#permito-config"></script>
A CDN sees the visitor's IP address when the file loads. Whether that is acceptable is your assessment.
Add the config and the script

Put both into , the config first:
<script type="application/json" id="permito-config"> { "config": { "consentVersion": "2026-10", "language": "de-CH", "maxAgeDays": 365, "categories": [ { "id": "necessary", "required": true }, { "id": "statistics" }, { "id": "marketing" } ], "services": [ { "id": "youtube", "name": "YouTube", "provider": "Google Ireland Ltd.", "category": "marketing" } ] }, "privacyPolicyUrl": "/datenschutz", "imprintUrl": "/impressum", "googleConsentMode": true, "consentModeDefault": true } </script> <script src="/assets/permito.global.js" data-config="#permito-config"></script>
The config object takes every option of the configuration that can be written as JSON. The banner appears until the visitor decides; afterwards a small button in the corner reopens the settings.

Markup-based blocking is on by default. Change type to text/plain and name the category or service:
<script type="text/plain" data-consent-category="statistics" data-consent-src="https://plausible.io/js/script.js" data-domain="example.com"></script>
See Blocking scripts and embeds for iframes and inline scripts.
Any element with data-permito-open opens the preference center, for example in the footer: Cookie-Einstellungen

Besides config, the JSON accepts:
Option | Default | Description
privacyPolicyUrl, imprintUrl | none | Links in the banner and dialog. position | "bottom" | bottom, top, bottom-left, bottom-right, center. theme | follows the system | "light" or "dark". preferencesButton | "bottom-left" | "bottom-right" or false to hide it. hideCustomize | false | Hide the "Settings" button in the banner. serviceToggles | true | Switches per service in the dialog. googleConsentMode | false | Send Consent Mode v2 updates. consentModeDefault | false | Push the Consent Mode default (denied) immediately. Load the script without defer in , before the Google tag. microsoftUet, clarity, matomo | false | Forward the decision to Microsoft UET, Microsoft Clarity and Matomo. See Microsoft UET, Clarity and Matomo. blockedElements | true | Activate blocked markup after consent. injectStyles | true | Insert the default stylesheet. Set false and load dist/styles.css yourself, e.g. for a strict CSP. styleNonce | none | CSP nonce for the injected . translations | none | Override texts, see Translations.
Colours and radii follow the same CSS variables as the React components, see Theming.
With a bundler but without React

The decision lives in a cookie, so any server can read it with two helpers from @permitojs/core:
readConsentFromCookieHeader(cookieHeader) returns the stored decision or null. readGpcFromHeaders(headers) returns true for Sec-GPC: 1.
Pass the decision as initialState, and the signal as globalPrivacyControl: { signal }, so the first render already knows what the visitor chose and gated content does not flash.

// src/hooks.server.ts import { readConsentFromCookieHeader, readGpcFromHeaders } from "@permitojs/core";
export const handle = async ({ event, resolve }) => { event.locals.consent = readConsentFromCookieHeader(event.request.headers.get("cookie")); event.locals.gpc = readGpcFromHeaders(event.request.headers); return resolve(event); };
export async function loader({ request }: LoaderFunctionArgs) { return { consent: readConsentFromCookieHeader(request.headers.get("cookie")), gpc: readGpcFromHeaders(request.headers), }; }

--- import { readConsentFromCookieHeader } from "@permitojs/core"; const consent = readConsentFromCookieHeader(Astro.request.headers.get("cookie")); const allowStatistics = consent?.categories.statistics === true; --- {allowStatistics && <script src="/analytics.js" />}
Astro pages are often static. For those, gate scripts in the browser with data-consent-category markup and the script tag UI instead of reading the cookie on the server.

const cookie = useRequestHeaders(["cookie"]).cookie; const consent = readConsentFromCookieHeader(cookie);
Expired or outdated decisions (maxAgeDays, a new consentVersion) are checked by the manager when you pass the state as initialState; reading the raw cookie alone does not check them.

consentStore(manager) | The whole snapshot plus hasConsent and hasServiceConsent categoryStore(manager, id) | true while the category is granted serviceStore(manager, id) | true while the service is granted needsConsentStore(manager) | true while the banner should be shown, only after the stored decision was read
Create the manager in the browser only (for example behind browser from $app/environment) or pass initialState from the server, see server frameworks.

Import the default theme once:
import "@permitojs/react/styles.css";

The variables are defined with zero specificity on :root and inherited, so you can override them on :root, on any wrapper, or on .pmt-root:

Banner, preference center and the preferences button render into document.body by default, so layouts with transform, filter or contain cannot clip them. Styles scoped to a wrapper (for example .tenant-a { --pmt-accent: … }) therefore do not reach them. Either:
put the variables on :root or , or pass an element inside your wrapper as portalContainer on the provider, or render in place with portal={false} on the component.
Keep "Accept all" and "Reject all" visually equal when you restyle them. Both use the class pmt-btn--choice.
Every component accepts className and unstyled. For a completely own UI, use the hooks (useConsent) and render your own markup.

Permito is a consent toolkit for websites built with React. It shows a banner, lets visitors choose categories and individual services, stores that decision, and makes sure third-party code only runs once it is allowed.

Package | Use it for
@permitojs/react | React and Next.js apps. Includes everything from the core. @permitojs/core | Any other stack, or your own UI. Framework-agnostic, no dependencies.

Opt-in by default. Only categories you mark as required are active before a decision. Opt-out exists, but only if you configure it. Equal choices. "Accept all" and "Reject all" are always shown together and styled identically. Data minimisation. The stored decision contains categories, services, versions, a timestamp and the source of the decision. No IP address, no user agent, no identifier. No external communication. The open-source packages never call a server. Accessibility. Keyboard operable, focus management, labelled controls, prefers-reduced-motion and dark mode support, tested with axe-core.

Permito is technical infrastructure, not legal advice. It does not tell you which services need consent, it does not scan your site and it cannot guarantee compliance with the GDPR, the Swiss revDSG or any other law. See Legal notes.

pnpm add @permitojs/react # or: npm install @permitojs/react

Permito is technical consent infrastructure. It is not legal advice, and using it does not make a website compliant with the GDPR, the ePrivacy rules, the Swiss revDSG or any other law.
You decide
which categories and services exist and whether a service needs consent (requiresConsent), which texts visitors see (the built-in texts are neutral defaults, not legally reviewed), whether and how long decisions are stored, and whether you need proof of consent, which mode applies in which region.
Permito does
not pre-select optional categories (unless you configure opt-out), show "Accept all" and "Reject all" with equal weight, keep gated code from loading before consent, store no personal data in the decision, make no network requests.
Please have your configuration and texts reviewed by a qualified person.

The banner and the preference center are role="dialog" with an accessible name. The preference center is modal: focus stays inside, Escape closes it, page scroll is locked, and focus returns to the element that opened it. Category switches are real switch controls with labels. "Reject all" and "Accept all" have the same size and weight. The banner moves focus to itself when it appears, so keyboard and screen reader users notice it. Turn that off with autoFocus: false if you handle it yourself. The blocked-embed placeholder has a visible text and real buttons.

Every pull request runs end-to-end tests in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. They include an axe-core scan against WCAG 2.0 to 2.2 level A and AA for the banner, the preference center and the blocked-embed placeholder, and a keyboard test for focus trapping and focus return.
An axe scan finds only part of all accessibility problems. It cannot judge whether a text makes sense or whether the reading order helps. Test with a keyboard and a screen reader on your own site, in your own theme: custom colors and your own texts can break contrast and wording.

The audit found that after closing the preference center, focus did not return to the floating settings button, because that button is removed while the dialog is open. Both the React components and the script tag UI now restore focus to it.
Manual check with a screen reader

Run this on your own site with at least one screen reader (VoiceOver with Safari on macOS or iOS, NVDA with Firefox or Chrome on Windows). It takes about ten minutes. Automated tests cannot do it.
Open the page in a private window. The banner announces itself as a dialog with its name, and the first thing read is its heading. Move through the banner with Tab. "Reject all" and "Accept all" are both reachable and both announced as buttons. Open the preference center. Focus moves into it, Tab stays inside, and the category switches are announced with name and state (on or off). Press Escape. The dialog closes and focus returns to the element that opened it. Change a switch, save, and reload. The state is announced as you left it. Check the blocked-embed placeholder, if you use one: the text tells what is blocked and the button is announced as a button. Repeat with your texts and your colors if you changed them.
Results of this check on your site belong to your own accessibility documentation. Permito's own test results do not replace it.

A purpose is the unit that systems outside the browser act on: the newsletter, ad personalisation, a CRM sync. Each one belongs to a category and has an id that is the same in the browser, in the stored decision and in the webhook.
interface ConsentPurposeDefinition { id: string;            // stable, used by your backend category: string;      // granting or declining the category sets the purpose name?: LocalizedText; description?: LocalizedText; }
Without purposes, every category is one purpose with the category's id. A visitor decides per category in the banner. Your code can narrow a granted category to fewer purposes with manager.setPurposeConsent(id, false): a purpose is granted while its category is granted and the purpose was not declined. Declining a category declines all its purposes, granting it again grants them all again. The built-in banner shows categories, not purposes.
A service can list the purposes it serves (purposes: ["newsletter"]). It runs only while its category and all of these purposes are granted.

Permito follows semantic versioning. From 1.0.0:
Patch releases (1.0.x) fix bugs and correct wording. They never change the stable API. Minor releases (1.x.0) add features. They never remove or change something listed as stable in API status. Service templates and translations can be added; the default category of an existing template does not change. Major releases (2.0.0, 3.0.0) can remove or change the stable API. Everything removed was marked @deprecated in at least one earlier minor release and is named in the release notes with a migration hint.
@permitojs/core and @permitojs/react share one version number and are released together.
The stored decision has its own schema number. A change to it comes with a migration that keeps existing decisions where it can, and is named in the release notes.

The latest minor release of the current major version gets bug fixes and security fixes. When a new major version appears, the last minor release of the previous major keeps getting bug fixes and security fixes for 12 months from the day the new major is released. 1.x is supported until 12 months after the release of 2.0.0.
There is no response-time guarantee for free issues. Permito Pro has its own terms.

Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub Security Advisories on the repository ("Report a vulnerability" on the Security tab). Do not open a public issue. We aim to acknowledge a report within 5 working days and to publish a fixed release and an advisory once a fix is available.

Scroll motion without the JavaScript tax: native CSS scroll timelines, spring and S-curve easings as CSS linear(), reduced motion by default. About 3 kB for a reveal.
Most scroll animations still run in JavaScript: a listener measures elements and changes styles on every frame. Browsers can now do this themselves with CSS scroll-driven animations. Sigmoid is a small layer on top of that platform feature. Reveals, parallax and scroll-linked effects run on native view and scroll timelines, and a tiny fallback with the same range maths covers browsers that do not have them yet.
With sigmoid.css you do not even need JavaScript: write data-sigmoid="fade-up" and the browser animates it. The easing curves are the other half: physically correct springs, the logistic S-curve and Bézier curves that work as JavaScript functions and as CSS linear(), also together with Motion, GSAP or Tailwind. When people ask their system for reduced motion, Sigmoid shows the content without moving it.

reveal, parallax, scrub and a reading progress bar on native CSS view and scroll timelines Staggered lists and grids with one option, also in CSS with --sigmoid-index track(): scroll progress as a number for counters, video or canvas story(): scroll stories with a pinned section and steps, in JavaScript, React or CSS Horizontal scrolling on the inline axis, for carousels and galleries splitText(): words and characters that arrive one after another, readable by screen readers Counters without JavaScript: data-sigmoid="count" Linked animations: one element drives others, and pinned sections with one attribute Zero-JavaScript mode: data-sigmoid attributes in one stylesheet A small fallback with the same range maths as the CSS spec, also inside scroll containers, tested against the native path in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit Physically correct springs, the logistic S-curve and Bézier curves as functions and as CSS linear() Curves usable with Motion, GSAP, CSS transitions and as a Tailwind CSS v4 theme A curve editor on packages.sweber.

Why not just use Motion or GSAP?

Both are excellent and do far more: layout animations, gestures, timelines. If you only need scroll-linked motion and good curves, Sigmoid lets the browser do the work and stays around 3 kB. Its easing curves also work inside Motion and GSAP.
How does it compare in size and speed?

A reveal is about 3 kB, GSAP with ScrollTrigger about 45 kB and Motion about 23 kB, all minified and gzipped. On a native timeline Sigmoid runs about 1 ms of JavaScript while scrolling. With hundreds of elements animating at once, Chromium's native path costs more main-thread time than GSAP in our headless test, and we say so in the benchmark. The script is in the repository.

Browsers with CSS scroll-driven animations, such as Chrome, Edge and Safari 26. Others, Firefox for now, get the JavaScript fallback with the same result. CI checks both paths in real Chromium, Firefox and WebKit on every change. The docs list the details.
Is there a Vue or Svelte package?

Yes. @sweberdev/sigmoid-vue has the v-reveal and v-parallax directives and composables, @sweberdev/sigmoid-svelte has the actions use:reveal, use:parallax, use:track and use:story. Install either next to @sweberdev/sigmoid. Astro needs no adapter, the docs have a guide.
Does it work with Next.js and Server Components?
Yes. The data-sigmoid attributes work in Server Components without client code. The React components are client components that render one element.
Reveals and parallax are skipped and the content is shown. Only the reading progress bar stays, because it moves only when the user scrolls.

The stylesheet defines every curve of ease on :root, so you can use them anywhere, also for transitions:
.button { transition: transform 0.4s var(--sigmoid-ease-bouncy); }

With Tailwind CSS 4: ease-(--sigmoid-ease-bouncy), or register them in @theme as --ease-bouncy: var(--sigmoid-ease-bouncy).

Name | Curve
ease.out | cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1), fast start and long landing; the default for reveals ease.inOut | cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1) ease.standard | cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1) ease.sigmoid | logistic S-curve, steepness 10 ease.smooth | spring without overshoot (perceived 0.5 s) ease.bouncy | spring with light overshoot (perceived 0.6 s) ease.wobbly | spring with a clear wobble (perceived 0.8 s) ease.linear | linear

spring({ duration: 0.6, bounce: 0.3 });               // perceptual, like SwiftUI spring({ stiffness: 170, damping: 26, mass: 1 });     // physical spring({ duration: 0.4, velocity: 4 });               // start with speed
The spring is solved analytically (under-, critically and overdamped) and ends when it stays within 0.1% of the target. In a scroll-driven animation the scroll range sets the length, the curve keeps its shape.

logistic(6);   // soft S logistic(14);  // sharp S
Normalised so that it starts exactly at 0 and ends exactly at 1.

bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1);               // same as cubic-bezier() in CSS easing((t) => 1 - (1 - t) ** 4);           // any function, CSS generated toLinear((t) => t * t, { tolerance: 0.001 }); // just the linear() string
toLinear samples the curve and removes every point that does not change the result by more than the tolerance (default 0.0015), so a spring needs 20 to 40 stops instead of hundreds. CSS linear() works in Chrome 113, Safari 17.2 and Firefox 112 and newer. Older browsers get the curve applied in JavaScript.

Where ViewTimeline and ScrollTimeline are missing, Sigmoid creates the same Web Animation, pauses it and sets its time from the scroll position on each animation frame. One passive listener serves all elements. The range maths follow the CSS spec, so native and fallback look the same. Like view(), the fallback measures each element against its nearest scroll container, so reveals inside a scrolling panel or a carousel work the same as on the page.
Pass fallback: true to force it, e.g. to compare both paths.

People with vestibular disorders can get dizzy or nauseous from motion they did not start, especially parallax and large movement. Operating systems have a setting for this, and browsers expose it as prefers-reduced-motion: reduce (WCAG 2.3.3, Animation from Interactions).
Sigmoid respects it by default:
| With reduced motion
data-sigmoid presets and parallax | not animated, content is shown reveal, parallax, scrub | no animation is created, animations is empty progress, data-sigmoid="progress" | stays on: it only reflects the scroll position
The presets animate from a hidden state to the element's own style, so skipping them always leaves the content visible.
To keep an animation that is essential, pass reducedMotion: "allow", and prefer a calmer variant, e.g. a fade instead of movement:
const calm = prefersReducedMotion(); reveal(".chart", { keyframes: calm ? "fade-in" : "fade-up", reducedMotion: "allow" });
In React, useReducedMotion() updates when the setting changes.

Most scroll animations on the web are still driven by JavaScript: a scroll listener or an IntersectionObserver measures elements and updates styles on every frame. Browsers can now do this themselves. With CSS scroll-driven animations an animation follows the scroll position on the compositor, without any script running.
Sigmoid is a small layer on top of that platform feature:

Native first. reveal(), parallax(), scrub() and progress() create Web Animations on a ViewTimeline or ScrollTimeline. The browser does the work. Zero JavaScript if you want. Add sigmoid.css and write data-sigmoid="fade-up". Modern browsers animate it with CSS alone. A fallback that stays small. Where scroll timelines are missing, one passive scroll listener drives the same animations. It computes progress with the same range maths as the CSS spec, so both paths look the same. Curves with character. Springs, the logistic S-curve and Bézier curves as one Easing object: call it in JavaScript or use it in CSS as linear(). The springs are physically correct and also report their natural duration. Reduced motion by default. When the user asks the system for less motion, reveals and parallax are skipped and content is simply shown. Small. About 3.1 kB min+gzip for reveal + init, 4.9 kB for everything. A size check in CI keeps it that way.

Sigmoid does scroll-linked motion and easing. It does not do layout animations, gestures, drag, SVG morphing or timelines with many steps. For those, Motion and GSAP are excellent. The easing curves of Sigmoid work with both of them, see Easing.
The sigmoid function is the S-shaped curve that starts slowly, moves decisively and settles softly. It is the shape most good motion has, and it is available here as ease.sigmoid.

Size is the minified and gzipped bundle of the snippet, without CSS. This is where Sigmoid is clearly smaller: the native path hands the work to the browser. "CSS only" needs no JavaScript at all. JavaScript is the script time while scrolling 150 steps. Sigmoid on a native timeline runs about 1 ms, because the browser drives the animation. The fallback is the same maths in JavaScript. GSAP ScrollTrigger and Motion run their code on every frame. Main-thread tasks include everything the main thread did: JavaScript, style recalculation and, in this headless Chromium without a GPU, painting. With 30 elements all libraries are close to each other. With 300 elements at the same time, Chromium updates every view timeline on the main thread and the native path costs more main-thread time than GSAP in this setup, even though almost none of it is JavaScript. Real devices with GPU compositing may differ. AOS fires an animation once and does not follow the scroll position, so it is not the same effect; it is in the table as a size reference.

What this means in practice: for the usual page, a few dozen animated elements, Sigmoid costs about as much main-thread time as GSAP and a fraction of the bytes. For very long lists with hundreds of elements animating at once, test on your target devices, and consider revealing only the elements that are close to the viewport.

Sigmoid follows semantic versioning. The API listed in this documentation is frozen as of 0.9.0, the release candidate: 1.0.0 will contain no API changes, only fixes found during the candidate phase. From 1.0.0 on:
Patch (1.0.x): bug fixes only. Minor (1.x.0): new features, new options with defaults that keep the old behaviour, new exports. Nothing breaks. Major (2.0.0): anything that can break existing code.

Does Summand replace the KoSIT validator?

Yes, for what the KoSIT validator checks: since 0.3.0 Summand first checks the official XML Schema (UBL 2.1 or CII D16B), then runs the same official Schematron files, and it passes the KoSIT test suite. Its schema check gives the same valid or invalid verdict as the Xerces engine KoSIT uses on more than 4,000 test documents. What it does not produce is KoSIT's HTML report format.

XRechnung 3.0 in UBL and CII, ZUGFeRD 2.x and Factur-X as PDF or XML, Peppol BIS and plain EN 16931 invoices. ZUGFeRD 1.0 predates EN 16931 and is reported as unsupported. Factur-X MINIMUM and BASIC WL are recognised but are not full invoices under EN 16931, which Summand says in the result.
Does an invoice that passes meet the German VAT rules?

Not automatically. Summand checks the technical rules of EN 16931 and XRechnung. Whether an invoice is correct for VAT purposes, for example the tax rate or an exemption, is a question for your accounting or tax adviser.
No. It runs where you call it: on your server, in your function or in the browser. Nothing is uploaded, and the Pro packages do not contact a licence server either.
Why are the rule sets under other licences?

Summand's code is MIT. The bundled rules are the official artefacts: EN 16931 from CEN under the EUPL 1.2 and XRechnung from KoSIT under the Apache License 2.0. Both allow this use; the notices ship with the package.

See CLI.
Validating invoices: options and the result in detail Profiles and rule sets: which rules run for XRechnung, ZUGFeRD and Factur-X In the browser: check uploads before they reach your server

Every input gives exactly one BatchResult:
Field | Content
index | Position of the input, starting at 0 name | The path, or the name you gave result | The ValidationResult of validateInvoice (set unless error is set). An invalid invoice is a result with result.valid === false. error | { code: "SUM-BATCH", message }, set instead of result when the input could not be processed: the file cannot be read (missing, a directory, no permission), the data could not be sent to the worker, or the worker failed. See SUM-BATCH.
Results arrive in input order, whichever file finishes first. The same input gives the same sequence for every concurrency, which makes runs comparable and reports reproducible. A slow file delays the results behind it, not the work: the other workers keep going up to the window of twice concurrency results.
Nothing is thrown per input. validateMany throws synchronously only for a concurrency that is not a positive integer (RangeError), and the iteration rejects when the signal aborts or when your own input iterable throws.

validateMany takes every option of validateInvoice (lang, ruleSets, schema, includeXml, ...), applied to every input, plus:
Option | Default | Effect
concurrency | min(4, number of CPU cores) | How many invoices are validated at the same time, one worker thread each. Workers are started when there is work for them, and a worker that dies is replaced. With 1, the invoices are validated one after another on the calling thread and no worker is started (useful for debugging and where worker threads are not available). signal | none | An AbortSignal. When it aborts, pending inputs are dropped, workers are terminated and the iteration rejects with the signal's reason.
The default is capped at 4 because validation is memory-hungry, see the measurements below; set a higher value if you have measured that it helps on your machine. Options are copied to the workers, so they must be plain data (no functions).

A script that wraps validateMany should do what summand validate does: exit 1 when some invoice is invalid, and 2 when some input has an error. An unreadable file must not look like a valid one.
let invalid = 0; let failed = 0; for await (const r of validateMany(files)) { if (r.error) failed++; else if (!r.result.valid) invalid++; } process.exitCode = failed ? 2 : invalid ? 1 : 0;

It depends on the invoices and, more than you would expect, on the machine. Measured numbers, the method and a control experiment are in Performance. In short, on our 4-core test container: about 1.5x for 1,000-line invoices, at most 1.26x for 100-line invoices, and slower than a plain loop for batches of small invoices, because each worker has to start and warm up. The speed-up is limited by memory bandwidth, not only by the number of cores.

There is no browser version of validateMany: browsers have no worker_threads and no file system access by path. Call validateInvoice for each file instead. For many files, use a few Web Workers yourself, each running validateInvoice (see In the browser), and keep the number of workers small for the reason above.

Command | Does
summand validate | Validate XML and PDF files summand extract [--out file.xml] | Write the embedded XML of a ZUGFeRD / Factur-X PDF summand leitweg | Check a Leitweg-ID and print the correct check digits summand --version | Print the version summand rules [--json] [--check [--fail-on-outdated]] | List the bundled rule sets with version, source, licence and rule count; --check asks whether newer releases exist (exit code 3 with --fail-on-outdated). Lists every bundled version, including older ones you can select. See Rule sets and versions.

Option | Effect
--json | One JSON result per line (JSON Lines) --rule-sets | Rule sets to apply, comma-separated, each optionally with a version: en16931,xrechnung@2.5.0. Default auto. An unknown name or version is a usage error (exit 2). See Rule sets and versions. --strict-extended | EXTENDED: EN 16931 violations are errors --no-schema | Skip the XML Schema (XSD) check --no-leitweg | Do not check the Leitweg-ID in the buyer reference --lang de | Messages and output in German (default en) --warnings-as-errors | Exit 1 on warnings too --quiet | Only the summary line per file

Code | Meaning
0 | Success: every invoice is valid 1 | An invoice is invalid (or has warnings with --warnings-as-errors), including input that is not an invoice at all 2 | The command could not run: unknown command or flag, missing arguments, unreadable file 3 | rules --check --fail-on-outdated: a newer release of a bundled rule set exists
The codes follow ESLint: 1 is a finding, 2 is an error running the command. If one of several files cannot be read, the others are still validated and the exit code is 2. To tell an invalid invoice from a failed run in a script, test for 1 and 2 separately. Details: Error codes.
--json prints one line per file: { "file": "invoice.xml", ...result }, where result is the ValidationResult. The field names are stable.

Summand 1.0.0 is the first stable release. From here on the stability policy below applies. The API is the one 0.9 had; the only breaking change is in the exit codes of the summand command.

The CLI now splits exit codes like ESLint. Before, exit code 1 meant both "an invoice is invalid" and "the command could not run". Now:
Situation | Before 1.0 | 1.0
Every invoice valid | 0 | 0 An invoice is invalid, warnings with --warnings-as-errors, or the input is not an invoice (SUM-FORMAT, SUM-XML, SUM-PDF) | 1 | 1 leitweg with an invalid ID | 1 | 1 Unknown command or flag, missing arguments (including --lang fr), no command at all | 1 | 2 A file that cannot be read (does not exist, no permission) | 1 | 2 extract on a file that is not a PDF or has no embedded XML | 1 | 2 rules --check --fail-on-outdated and a newer release exists | 3 | 3
Also, validate no longer stops at the first unreadable file: it validates the other files, reports the unreadable one on stderr and exits with 2 (an error wins over findings).
What to do with your scripts.

summand validate ... | | exit 1 or if ! summand validate ...: nothing to change; any non-zero code still fails. [ $? -eq 1 ] or if [ "$code" == 1 ] to detect "invoice invalid": that now matches only real findings. A typo in a path used to look like an invalid invoice; it is now 2. Decide what 2 should mean in your pipeline (usually: fail the build and fix the script), and handle it explicitly:
summand validate invoices/*.xml case $? in 0) echo "all valid" ;; 1) echo "invalid invoices found"; exit 1 ;; *) echo "summand could not run"; exit 2 ;; esac
Code that calls runCli receives the same numbers. EXIT_CODES is internal; do not import it. Code that treated "not 0" as "invalid invoice" and showed that to users should now tell exit 2 apart, or read valid from --json output as before. --json output itself is unchanged.

From 1.0.0 Summand follows Semantic Versioning. MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH:
Major (2.0.0): anything listed under covered below is removed, renamed or changes its meaning. Minor (1.1.0): additions, new SUM- codes, new rule set releases, deprecations. Patch (1.0.1): bug fixes, documentation, dependency updates, no new features.

Every export of @sweberdev/summand, @sweberdev/summand/rules-check and @sweberdev/summand/cli that is not marked @beta: names, parameters, return and option types, and the behaviour the TSDoc and these docs describe. Adding an optional option or a field to a result is a minor change, so do not treat results as closed objects; add default branches when you switch on ProfileId, SchemaFindingKind or Syntax. The ValidationResult and ValidationMessage shape, including the field names of the --json output ({ file, ...result }). The SUM- codes: their ids, their severities and what they mean. A code is never reused. New codes appear in minor releases, see below. The summand command: commands, flags and the exit codes 0, 1, 2 and 3. New commands and flags are minor; a flag never changes meaning. The package entry points (exports of package.json) and the summand binary. Node.js 22 and newer since 2.0.0 (1.x: Node.js 20). Dropping a Node.js version is a major change.

Advanced exports (@beta): the compiled rule and schema formats (compileSchematron, runSchematron, ruleSet, SchemaModel), the XML node tree (parseXml, XNode, ...) and the whole @sweberdev/summand/xpath entry point. They may change in a minor release, always with a note in the changelog, never in a patch. The wording of message texts in either language. Match on id, severity and location. The order of messages inside errors, warnings and infos, except that schema errors (SUM-XSD) come first. durationMs, the layout of the dist folder, and the compiled JSON files in src. The ids and wording of rules that come from the bundled rule sets (BR-CO-15, BR-DE-15, ...): they are the upstream's, see below.

A deprecated export keeps working for at least the rest of the major version. Its TSDoc names the replacement and the version that removes it (@deprecated Use ... Removed in 2.0.0.), the changelog lists it, and the docs name it on the API page. Deprecated exports are removed only in a major release.
Rule set updates and verdict changes

The verdict for an invoice depends on the bundled rule sets (EN 16931 validation artefacts and XRechnung Schematron) and XML Schemas. They are fixed per Summand version: the same invoice gives the same result with the same Summand version, and result.ruleSets and result.schemas record the versions used, so you can store them next to a verdict.
A new upstream release of a rule set is released as a minor version of Summand, never as a patch and never inside a major version without a note. Upstream releases can add rules, remove rules, change a rule's text or change severity, so an invoice that was valid can become invalid and the reverse. This is the whole point of keeping up with the standard, so it is not a breaking change in the SemVer sense. It is always communicated:
Rule set updates and verdict changes

The changelog entry of the release has the heading Rule set update with the old and new version of every rule set and a link to the upstream release notes. It states the verdict changes we know of: rules added, removed or changed in severity, and which invoices are affected. We run the full test fixtures (CEN unit tests, KoSIT test suite) with the old and the new rule set and report the differences. summand rules and result.ruleSets show the versions; summand rules --check tells you when upstream is ahead of your Summand version.
Any other release that can change the verdict of some invoice carries a Verdict changes section in its changelog entry:
Release | Allowed to change verdicts?
Patch | Only to fix a deviation from the reference (the official rule set or the KoSIT validator): Summand was wrong. Listed under Verdict changes. Minor | New rule set releases, new SUM- checks, new schema versions. Listed under Rule set update or Verdict changes. Major | Anything, listed in the migration notes.
Rule set updates and verdict changes

If you need verdicts that never change, pin the exact version of @sweberdev/summand ("@sweberdev/summand": "1.4.2", no ^) and update on your schedule. If you want to be warned before a rule set update changes your results, run summand rules --check --fail-on-outdated in CI: it exits with code 3 as soon as upstream is ahead of the bundled version.

2.0.0 is a clean-up release. It removes everything that 1.1 and 1.0 deprecated, raises the minimum Node.js version and writes down the shape of a validation message as a contract. It adds no rules and changes no rule set: the same invoice gives the same verdict as with 1.1.0 and the same options. If you already use ruleSets and no deprecated exports, the only thing to check is your Node.js version.

Change | Affects you if | Replacement
Node.js 22 or newer is required (engines.node is >=22; 1.x said >=20) | you run Node.js 20 or older | Upgrade Node.js. Browsers, Deno, Bun and edge runtimes are not affected by this line. ValidateOptions.xrechnung removed | you pass xrechnung: true or false to validateInvoice or validateMany | ruleSets: ["en16931", "xrechnung"]; just drop xrechnung: false CLI flag --xrechnung removed | a script runs summand validate --xrechnung | --rule-sets en16931,xrechnung Info SUM-DEPRECATED removed | you filter or assert on this id | Nothing: no result contains it any more Type CheckOptions removed from @sweberdev/summand/rules-check | you import CheckOptions | RuleSetCheckOptions (the same type) ruleSetsFor(detection) takes no second argument | you called ruleSetsFor(detection, { xrechnung }) | Pass the rule sets you want to ruleSets instead
There is nothing else in this list. In particular the SUM- codes other than SUM-DEPRECATED, the names of the fields of results, the exit codes and the --json output are unchanged.

Check Node.js. node --version must print v22 or newer, locally, in CI and in your deployment image. Set "engines": { "node": ">=22" } in your own package if it depends on Summand. Move to 1.1.0 first if you are not there yet, and fix what the deprecation notes (SUM-DEPRECATED in result.infos, the line on stderr) point at. With 1.1.0 and no SUM-DEPRECATED in your results you are done with steps 3 and 4. Install 2.0.0: npm install @sweberdev/summand@2. Run your tests and your type check. TypeScript reports every removed option and type. JavaScript does not, see the first removal below.

xrechnung: true forced the XRechnung rules on top of EN 16931 for an invoice that does not declare XRechnung. ruleSets does the same and also lets you pick a version.
// 1.x validateInvoice(xml, { xrechnung: true }); validateInvoice(xml, { xrechnung: false }); // the default
// 2.0 validateInvoice(xml, { ruleSets: ["en16931", "xrechnung"] }); validateInvoice(xml); // ruleSets: "auto" is the default
# 1.x summand validate --xrechnung invoice.xml
# 2.0 summand validate --rule-sets en16931,xrechnung invoice.xml
A test in 1.1 showed that both forms give identical results, including for profiles that are not EN 16931 compliant (MINIMUM, BASIC WL), where neither form applies a rule set.
JavaScript callers. The library checks the removed option at run time: validateInvoice returns the error SUM-RULESET ("The option xrechnung was removed in 2.0.0") instead of running with fewer rules, so a forgotten xrechnung: true cannot silently weaken a check. TypeScript users get a compile error. The CLI treats --xrechnung as a usage error with exit code 2 and nothing is validated.

Summand 1.x supported Node.js 20. 2.0 requires Node.js 22 or newer: engines is >=22, and CI runs the full suite on Node.js 22 and 24. Package managers that enforce engines (pnpm with engine-strict, npm with engine-strict=true) refuse to install on older versions; others print a warning. The browser build is not tied to a Node.js version: the compiled code targets ES2022.
Versions older than 22 are not tested any more. If 2.0 happens to run there, that is not supported.

Result messages (errors, warnings, infos) already had id, severity and ruleSet in 1.x. 2.0 states them as the contract and the test suite checks it on real results. No field was renamed or added; in particular the code is still called id, not code, so no code that reads results needs to change.
Field | Contract in 2.0
id | The stable code. A rule id of a bundled rule set (BR-CO-10, BR-DE-15, UBL-CR-646) or a SUM- code. SUM- codes are never renamed or reused. severity | "error", "warning" or "info", always equal to the list the message is in. ruleSet | "en16931-ubl", "en16931-cii", "xrechnung-ubl", "xrechnung-cii" or "summand". "summand" if and only if the id starts with SUM-.
Details and the full code list: Error codes. What did change in the catalogue: SUM-DEPRECATED is gone. The other codes (SUM-XML, SUM-FORMAT, SUM-PDF, SUM-XSD, SUM-PROFILE, SUM-EXTENDED, SUM-LEITWEG, SUM-PDF-LEVEL, SUM-RULESET, SUM-BATCH) keep their ids, severities and meanings.

Be clear about this before you rely on it:
No Peppol Schematron. The Peppol BIS Billing 3.0 rules (PEPPOL-EN16931-R...) are not bundled. Peppol invoices are recognised as a profile and checked against EN 16931 only. Selecting peppol in ruleSets is an error (SUM-RULESET). The 1.1 notes announced Peppol rule sets as planned; they are not part of 2.0. No Factur-X EXTENDED Schematron. EXTENDED invoices are checked against EN 16931, with violations as warnings by default and errors with extended: "strict". The EXTENDED-specific rules are not checked. The reason is unchanged: we cannot confirm the licence of the FNFE-MPE files, see Rule sets.
Corrections for 1.x are planned for 12 months after the release of 2.0.0, as announced with 1.1.0.

import { extractInvoiceXml, readPdf } from "@sweberdev/summand";
const found = extractInvoiceXml(bytes); found?.xml;  // the invoice XML found?.name; // "factur-x.xml"
readPdf(bytes).files; // all embedded files with name, MIME type and data
Summand looks at all embedded files and takes the one with a known invoice file name, otherwise the first one that is a UBL or CII invoice. Compressed object streams and cross-reference streams are supported.
What is checked about the PDF

Whether it contains an invoice at all (SUM-PDF if not: a plain PDF is not an e-invoice). Whether the profile in the XMP metadata (fx:ConformanceLevel) matches the XML (SUM-PDF-LEVEL warning). Encrypted PDFs are not supported.
PDF/A-3 conformance itself (fonts, colour profiles, metadata schema) is not checked. Use veraPDF for that if you create PDFs.

Most invoices have a handful of lines and validate in a few milliseconds to a few tens of milliseconds. This page is about the other end: invoices with hundreds or thousands of lines, such as utility bills or consolidated billing.

Median of 5 runs after one warm-up run (3 runs for 5,000 lines), validateInvoice on a string, all phases on (XML Schema, EN 16931 rules, XRechnung rules), in milliseconds. Node 22.22.0 on an Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz with 4 virtual cores (a cloud container), Linux 6.18. Your machine will differ, compare the ratios rather than the absolute values.
Invoice | Size | Before (0.3.0) | After | Faster
UBL XRechnung, 100 lines | 111 KB | 417 | 60 | 6.9x UBL EN 16931, 100 lines | 111 KB | 316 | 35 | 9.1x CII XRechnung, 100 lines | 195 KB | 476 | 40 | 12x CII EN 16931, 100 lines | 195 KB | 470 | 37 | 12.6x UBL XRechnung, 1,000 lines | 1.1 MB | 5,988 | 675 | 8.9x UBL EN 16931, 1,000 lines | 1.1 MB | 5,519 | 504 | 11x CII XRechnung, 1,000 lines | 1.9 MB | 29,819 | 420 | 71x CII EN 16931, 1,000 lines | 1.9 MB | 28,884 | 401 | 72x UBL XRechnung, 5,000 lines | 5.4 MB | fails (stack overflow) | 4,552 | - UBL EN 16931, 5,000 lines | 5.4 MB | fails (stack overflow) | 3,150 | - CII XRechnung, 5,000 lines | 9.5 MB | fails (stack overflow) | 2,467 | - CII EN 16931, 5,000 lines | 9.5 MB | fails (stack overflow) | 2,382 | -

At 1,000 lines the gain is between 9x and 72x. Not every part got faster: XML parsing (about 40 to 50 ms for 1,000 lines) and the XML Schema check (10 to 25 ms) were never the bottleneck and are unchanged. The 100-line values include the cost of the first calls (JIT), so their ratio is smaller than it would be for a long-running process.
Before this change, the EN 16931 rules took 4.5 to 30 seconds at 1,000 lines because many rules start with //cac:InvoiceLine or //ram:IncludedSupplyChainTradeLineItem and then look at the whole document again for every line, which is quadratic. At 5,000 lines the old engine did not finish at all: it ran out of stack space while collecting nodes of the document. That is fixed.
Time still grows faster than the number of lines (UBL XRechnung: 675 ms at 1,000 lines, 4.6 s at 5,000), so very large invoices are not free. Time per line is roughly 0.5 to 1 ms for UBL and 0.4 to 0.5 ms for CII in this measurement.
Verdicts and messages did not change. All 1,142 CEN unit tests, the KoSIT test suite and the XML Schema verdict tests pass unchanged.

The XPath engine indexes a document once by element and attribute name, so //name is a lookup in document order instead of a walk through every node. Absolute paths that depend only on the document (/a/b/c/@x, no variables) are evaluated once per validation run and reused by every rule that repeats them. Collecting and sorting nodes no longer copies arrays more often than needed, and steps without predicates do not build an evaluation context.

The benchmark builds invoices of any size from the sample invoices of the XRechnung test suite and times each phase. It is not part of the CI run.
cd packages/core pnpm bench                                  # 100, 1,000 and 5,000 lines, 7 runs each pnpm bench --runs 11 --sizes 100,1000 pnpm bench --json                           # machine-readable
A test (test/performance.test.ts) validates 1,000 lines in UBL and CII with a limit of 10 seconds. That is about 10 to 25 times the normal time on the machine above, so it passes on slow CI runners but fails if the quadratic behaviour comes back.

For batches there is validateMany (@sweberdev/summand/batch), see Validating many invoices. It runs the same validation in a pool of worker threads. The numbers below show what that buys and what it does not.
Whole batch, in milliseconds, median of 7 runs after one warm-up run. Every run reads the files from disk and validates each with all phases on (XML Schema, EN 16931 rules, XRechnung rules); the pool, including starting its worker threads, is created anew in every run. "Loop" is a plain for loop with validateInvoice on the calling thread, which is already warm from the warm-up run; validateMany(n) is concurrency: n, where 1 means the calling thread without workers. Node 22.22.0 on an Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz with 4 available cores (a cloud container), Linux 6.18.
Batch | Loop | validateMany(1) | validateMany(2) | validateMany(3) | validateMany(4)
200 small invoices (5 to 25 KB) | 1,127 | 1,187 | 1,466 | 1,592 | 1,693 40 invoices with 100 lines (110 to 195 KB) | 2,589 | 2,467 | 2,049 | 2,281 | 2,793 8 invoices with 1,000 lines (1.1 to 1.9 MB) | 5,052 | 5,020 | 3,410 | 3,393 | 3,577
Speed-up against the loop (above 1 is faster):
Batch | (1) | (2) | (3) | (4)

200 small invoices | 0.95x | 0.77x | 0.71x | 0.67x 40 invoices with 100 lines | 1.05x | 1.26x | 1.14x | 0.93x 8 invoices with 1,000 lines | 1.01x | 1.48x | 1.49x | 1.41x
What this says, honestly:

On this machine the pool helps only for large invoices, by about 1.5x with 2 to 4 workers, and not by 4x on 4 cores. For 100-line invoices the gain is at most 1.26x, and for small invoices the pool is slower than the loop. A worker has to start, load the rule sets and run its first invoices unoptimised, which costs a few hundred milliseconds per batch; results also have to be copied back to the calling thread. If the whole batch takes about a second sequentially, use concurrency: 1 or the plain loop. The limit is not the pool alone. As a control we validated the same eight 1,000-line files in plain Node processes without any pool: 8 files in one process took 5.8 to 6.9 s; the same files split over 4 separate processes (2 files each) took between 3.0 and 6.4 s per process in four attempts, so 4 processes gave between about 1x and about 2x. On this container validation is limited by memory bandwidth and shared resources, and the timings vary from run to run. A CPU-only loop scales perfectly on the same container (4 processes took as long as 1), so the cores are real; the workload is memory-hungry (it builds a tree of the whole XML document and a node index).

Expect better scaling on a machine with more memory bandwidth per core, and measure on yours. An earlier run of the same benchmark (5 runs, concurrency 1, 2 and 4) gave the same picture: 1.0x to 1.5x for 1,000-line invoices, 1.0x to 1.2x for 100 lines, 0.74x to 1.2x for small invoices. Memory per worker is that of one validation, so a large concurrency multiplies the peak memory of big invoices; this is the second reason the default is capped at min(4, cores).
The benefit that does not depend on the machine is that the calling thread stays free (your server or UI keeps responding during a long batch) and that results can be streamed in order while the batch is still running.

cd packages/core pnpm build                                 # the workers load dist/batch-worker.js pnpm bench:batch                           # three batches, concurrency 1, 2 and 4, 5 runs each pnpm bench:batch --runs 7 --concurrency 1,2,3,4 pnpm bench:batch --json                    # machine-readable, with the machine description
The batches are built from the sample invoices of the XRechnung test suite (small), and from generated invoices with 100 and 1,000 lines (the same generator as pnpm bench). Compare the ratios and run it on the hardware you will deploy on.

Summand reads the specification identifier (BT-24: cbc:CustomizationID in UBL, GuidelineSpecifiedDocumentContextParameter/ram:ID in CII) and picks the rule sets:
Profile | Recognised by | Rule sets
XRechnung 3.0 | …#compliant#urn:xeinkauf.de:kosit:xrechnung_3.0 | EN 16931 + XRechnung XRechnung Extension | …#conformant#urn:xeinkauf.de:kosit:extension:xrechnung_3.0 | EN 16931 + XRechnung, with KoSIT's relaxed levels XRechnung CVD | …#compliant#urn:xeinkauf.de:kosit:xrechnung:cvd_… | EN 16931 + XRechnung ZUGFeRD / Factur-X EN 16931 (COMFORT) | urn:cen.eu:en16931:2017 | EN 16931 ZUGFeRD / Factur-X BASIC | …:factur-x.eu:1p0:basic | EN 16931 ZUGFeRD / Factur-X EXTENDED | …:factur-x.eu:1p0:extended | EN 16931, errors reported as warnings by default Peppol BIS Billing 3.0 | …peppol… | EN 16931 (Peppol rules not included yet) ZUGFeRD / Factur-X MINIMUM, BASIC WL | …:minimum, …:basicwl | none; reported as error SUM-PROFILE anything else | | EN 16931, with warning SUM-PROFILE
The EN 16931 rule set follows the syntax: en16931-ubl for UBL Invoice and Credit Note, en16931-cii for CII. The same goes for XRechnung.

These two Factur-X profiles leave out the invoice lines and other information EN 16931 requires. They are booking aids, not e-invoices: in Germany they do not count as an e-invoice under § 14 UStG since 2025. Summand reports them as invalid without running the rules.

The KoSIT validator configuration for XRechnung changes the severity of some EN 16931 rules, for example BR-CL-21 (item classification code list) becomes a warning, and for the extension BR-CO-16 becomes an information. Summand applies the same changes when the XRechnung rules run, so results match the KoSIT validator.

Summand checks EXTENDED invoices against EN 16931 only. The EXTENDED-specific Schematron of FNFE-MPE is not bundled, because its licence could not be confirmed, see Not included: Factur-X EXTENDED Schematron. Violations of EN 16931 are warnings by default (extended: "lenient") and errors with extended: "strict".

Summand bundles the official rule sets: the CEN EN 16931 validation artefacts and the KoSIT XRechnung Schematron, each for UBL and for CII. They are fixed per Summand release, so the same invoice gives the same result with the same Summand version. Since 1.1.0 you can also choose which rule sets run and, where more than one version is bundled, which version.

The ruleSets option of validateInvoice (CLI: --rule-sets) takes "auto" or a list of rule set names.
import { validateInvoice } from "@sweberdev/summand";
validateInvoice(xml);                                   // same as ruleSets: "auto" (the default) validateInvoice(xml, { ruleSets: ["en16931"] });        // EN 16931 only, even for XRechnung invoices validateInvoice(xml, { ruleSets: ["en16931", "xrechnung"] });   // both, even if the invoice does not declare XRechnung validateInvoice(xml, { ruleSets: ["en16931", "xrechnung@2.5.0"] }); // an older bundled XRechnung release
summand validate --rule-sets en16931,xrechnung@2.5.0 invoice.xml
Value | Meaning

"auto" (default) | What Summand always did: EN 16931 for the detected syntax, plus the XRechnung rules when the invoice declares XRechnung (see Profiles). No rule set for profiles that are not EN 16931 compliant (MINIMUM, BASIC WL), which are reported with SUM-PROFILE. "en16931", "xrechnung" | The rule set for the syntax of the document: the UBL rule set for UBL, the CII rule set for CII. "en16931-ubl", "en16931-cii", "xrechnung-ubl", "xrechnung-cii" | One syntax-specific rule set, applied as named. These are the ids that appear in result.ruleSets and in each message's ruleSet. They worked before 1.1.0 and are not deprecated. " @ " | A bundled version of that rule set, e.g. "xrechnung@2.5.0"; "xrechnung@v2.5.0" (the upstream release name) is accepted too. Without @ the default version applies.

A list applies exactly the rule sets named, in that order; it does not add the rule sets "auto" would add. Family names ("en16931", "xrechnung") follow the same profile guard as "auto": for MINIMUM and BASIC WL no rule set runs. An unknown name or version is not guessed: the result has the error SUM-RULESET (see the error codes), lists the versions that are bundled and no rule set runs. The CLI reports it as a usage error (exit code 2) before it reads any file.
result.ruleSets always lists the rule sets and versions that really ran, so a stored verdict says which versions produced it.
Pinning a version only for XRechnung invoices
The boolean xrechnung option and the --xrechnung flag of 1.x were removed in 2.0.0. Use ruleSets: ["en16931", "xrechnung"] / --rule-sets en16931,xrechnung, see Migrating to 2.0.

Rule set | Default version | Also bundled
en16931 (UBL, CII) | 1.3.16 | none xrechnung (UBL, CII) | 2.6.0 (XRechnung 3.0) | 2.5.0 (XRechnung 3.0.x, released 2026-01-31)
Only these. Other releases of the two upstream projects are not bundled, and ruleSets: ["en16931@1.3.15"] is an error. Each additional version adds to the package size and to the browser bundle (the older XRechnung release is about 60 KB of JSON, 15 KB gzipped), so versions are added deliberately, not for every upstream release.
What the older XRechnung release means in practice:

It is an XRechnung Schematron release; the EN 16931 rules stay at 1.3.16 whichever XRechnung version you pick. KoSIT's own configuration for 2.5.0 paired it with EN 16931 1.3.15, which is not bundled, so xrechnung@2.5.0 is not a reproduction of the KoSIT validator of January 2026, only of its XRechnung rules. The KoSIT severity changes (for example BR-CL-21 as a warning) are applied in the version of the validator configuration that matches 2.6.0 for both XRechnung versions, because they are tied to the EN 16931 rules, which are the same. Differences between 2.5.0 and 2.6.0 that we found by comparing the compiled rules: BR-TMP-2 is an error in 2.6.0 and was a warning in 2.5.0; BR-TMP-6 (UBL dates must be YYYY-MM-DD) and BR-TMP-4, BR-TMP-5, BR-TMP-7 (CII) exist only in 2.6.0; the text of BR-DE-19 and BR-DE-20 changed (IBAN check moved into a function); the lists of identifier scheme codes (ICD, EAS) gained codes in 2.6.0. The 54 invoices of the KoSIT test suite and the 349 instances of the 2.5.0 release give the same verdicts with both versions; the differences show on invoices that hit these rules.

The Schematron of the older release is vendored unchanged in packages/core/rules-src/xrechnung-2.5.0/ under the same Apache-2.0 licence as 2.6.0 (see NOTICE.md).
Use an older version to reproduce a verdict that was given under it, or to validate an invoice against the rules in force when it was issued. For new invoices use the default. A removal of a bundled version is a deprecation first.

The FNFE-MPE Schematron for Factur-X EXTENDED is not bundled. We checked when preparing 1.1.0: the FNFE-MPE site (fnfe-mpe.org) and its GitHub organisation could not be fetched from our build environment, and the copies of these files that we could reach (inside the Mustang project) carry no licence statement of their own; Mustang's Apache-2.0 licence covers Mustang, it does not state the terms of FNFE-MPE's files. We do not redistribute files whose licence we cannot confirm from the publisher. The files also use code lists loaded at run time from separate XML files, which the engine does not support yet.
So the behaviour is unchanged: EXTENDED invoices are checked against EN 16931, whose violations are warnings by default because EXTENDED may go beyond EN 16931, and errors with extended: "strict" (CLI --strict-extended). Summand does not check the EXTENDED-specific rules. If the publisher confirms in writing that the files may be redistributed (or publishes them under a clear open licence), they can be added as a further rule set in a minor release.
