--json prints the same information for scripts. In code:
import { ruleSetInfo } from "@sweberdev/summand";

for (const set of ruleSetInfo()) console.log(set.id, set.version, set.rules); // the defaults ruleSetInfo("xrechnung-ubl");                  // the default version of one rule set ruleSetInfo({ versions: "all" });              // every bundled version, defaults first ruleSetInfo("xrechnung-ubl", "2.5.0");         // one bundled version, or undefined
Each entry has id, name, version, release (the upstream release the files come from), publisher, source (URL), license (SPDX) and rules. A rule is one Schematron assertion, the checks that carry a rule id such as BR-CO-10. The list holds no build date, so builds stay reproducible. RULE_SETS is the default versions keyed by id, and every validateInvoice result lists the rule sets it applied (result.ruleSets) with these fields.
The data comes from packages/core/rules-src/sources.json. pnpm rules writes it into src/rules/info.json together with the rule counts and fails when the version stated in the vendored EN 16931 files or in NOTICE.md does not match.

npx @sweberdev/summand rules --check
Rule set       Version  Rules  Licence     Publisher  Source  Used     Update en16931-ubl    1.3.16   979    EUPL-1.2    ...                default  up to date xrechnung-ubl  v2.6.0   56     Apache-2.0  ...                default  newer release available: v2.7.0 xrechnung-ubl  v2.5.0   55     Apache-2.0  ...                on request (@2.5.0)  older version, not compared
For each default version it prints up to date, newer release available: or could not check: ; bundled older versions are listed as older version, not compared and never make --fail-on-outdated exit with 3. It reads the public release list of the two upstream GitHub repositories and compares it with the bundled version. It never downloads or installs anything and sends nothing about your invoices; the only requests are GET https://api.github.com/repos/ / /releases.
Exit code | Meaning
0 | Everything is up to date, or the sources could not be reached 3 | With --fail-on-outdated: a newer release exists

A newer upstream release is not installed by this command. Rule sets change with a new Summand version, which is the only way the results of your validations change. Without a token the GitHub API allows 60 requests per hour and IP address; set SUMMANDGITHUBTOKEN to send a token (to api.github.com only) when you run the check from a busy CI network.

The Summand repository runs this check every Monday (.github/workflows/rules-check.yml) and opens or updates one issue per upstream project when a newer release exists. It uses only the default GITHUB_TOKEN with issues: write.

Syntax | Schema
UBL Invoice, UBL CreditNote | OASIS UBL 2.1 (ubl-2.1) UN/CEFACT CrossIndustryInvoice (XRechnung CII, ZUGFeRD, Factur-X) | UN/CEFACT CII 100.D16B, SCRDM subset with uncoupled code lists (cii-d16b)
These are the schemas EN 16931 1.3.16 and the KoSIT configuration for XRechnung 3.0 use. Code lists are not part of them; codes are checked by the Schematron rules. The schema is picked from the root element, independent of the profile, so ZUGFeRD / Factur-X invoices of every profile are checked against CII D16B.

Every violation is an error with the id SUM-XSD, the XPath of the element or attribute and its line. With lang: "de" (CLI --lang de) the messages are in German, for example Pflichtelement cbc:ID fehlt in ubl:Invoice (erwartet vor cbc:IssueDate).; element names, values and locations stay the same.
Problem | Example message

Unknown element | cbc:Colour is not allowed in ubl:Invoice (expected cbc:IssueTime, cbc:DueDate, …, cac:AccountingSupplierParty). Missing required element | Required element cbc:ID is missing in ubl:Invoice (expected before cbc:IssueDate). Wrong order | cbc:ID is in the wrong position in ubl:Invoice: it must come before cbc:IssueDate. Too many occurrences | cbc:IssueDate occurs too often in ubl:Invoice (at most 1 allowed). Missing required attribute | Required attribute currencyID is missing on cbc:LineExtensionAmount. Unknown attribute | Attribute currency is not allowed on cbc:LineExtensionAmount. Fixed attribute value | Attribute listID on ram:TypeCode must have the fixed value "1001", found "UNTDID 1001". Value format | Value "314,86" of cbc:LineExtensionAmount is not a valid xs:decimal (expected a decimal number such as 123.45). Text or child elements where they do not belong | cac:AccountingSupplierParty must not contain text, only child elements (found "oops").

The built-in types the schemas use are checked as XML Schema defines them: xs:decimal, xs:date (including the number of days in the month and the time zone), xs:time, xs:dateTime, xs:boolean, xs:base64Binary (including padding), xs:language and the string types; facets (minLength, maxLength and the others) are checked as well.
The Schematron rules still run when the schema check fails, so you see every problem at once. Turn the schema check off with validateInvoice(xml, { schema: false }) or summand validate --no-schema.
Using the schema check on its own

The verdict (valid or not) was compared with Xerces, the schema validator the KoSIT validator uses, on all test invoices and on about 2,800 modified ones, with the same result for every document. The messages differ: Xerces stops checking an element's content at the first problem, Summand reports each problem it finds, with a readable text instead of cvc-complex-type.2.4.a. A few things are not checked:
UBL signatures. ext:ExtensionContent is validated laxly as the schema says (elements with a declaration in the bundled schema are checked, anything else is accepted), but the UBL signature schemas (sig:, sac:, sbc:, XML Signature, XAdES) are not bundled, so signature content is not checked. Lax validation also only knows the UBL declarations an Invoice or CreditNote can contain. xsi:type. An element that replaces its type with xsi:type is not checked further. Invoices do not use it. xs:anyURI is accepted as written, like Xerces does for nearly every value.

import { validateInvoice } from "@sweberdev/summand";
const result = validateInvoice(input, options);

Input | Treated as
string | Invoice XML Uint8Array or ArrayBuffer starting with %PDF- | ZUGFeRD / Factur-X PDF; the embedded XML is validated other Uint8Array or ArrayBuffer | XML, decoded by its BOM or the encoding of the XML declaration (UTF-8 by default)
validateInvoice is synchronous and never throws for bad input: malformed XML, a PDF without invoice, or a document that is not an invoice come back as an error in the result.

Option | Default | Effect
ruleSets | "auto" | Rule sets to apply, e.g. ["en16931", "xrechnung"] or ["en16931", "xrechnung@2.5.0"] for a bundled older version. "auto" picks them from the syntax and profile, see Profiles and Rule sets and versions. extended | "lenient" | ZUGFeRD / Factur-X EXTENDED: report EN 16931 violations as warnings ("lenient") or as errors ("strict"). schema | true | Check the XML Schema (UBL 2.1 or CII D16B) before the Schematron rules. Violations are errors with the id SUM-XSD. See XML Schema. leitwegId | true | Warn when the buyer reference looks like a Leitweg-ID but has wrong check digits. includeXml | false | Return the validated XML in result.xml (handy for PDFs). lang | "en" | Language of the messages: "en" or "de". German covers every EN 16931 rule and Summand's own checks; the XRechnung rules are German in the original. Rule ids, locations and lines are the same in both languages.

Field | Content
valid | true when errors is empty syntax | "ubl-invoice", "ubl-creditnote" or "cii" profile | id, label, the specification identifier (BT-24) and whether the profile is EN 16931 compliant source | type ("xml" or "pdf"), the name of the embedded file and the conformance level from the PDF metadata ruleSets | Applied rule sets with the same data as ruleSetInfo(): name, version, release, publisher, source, licence and rule count, see Rule sets and versions schemas | XML Schemas the invoice was checked against (ubl-2.1 or cii-d16b), with name, version, source and licence; empty with schema: false errors, warnings, infos | Messages, see below summary | Invoice number, type, dates, currency, buyer reference, seller and buyer (name, VAT ID, country), totals and the number of lines durationMs | Time taken
Each message has:
Field | Example

id | "BR-CO-15", "BR-DE-15", "UBL-CR-646", "SUM-PDF" severity | "error", "warning" or "info" message | The rule's text as published (EN 16931 rules in English, XRechnung rules in German) location | XPath of the element, e.g. /Invoice/cac:InvoiceLine[2]/cac:Price line | Line in the XML ruleSet | "en16931-ubl", "xrechnung-cii", … or "summand" evaluationError | Set when the rule could not be evaluated, e.g. an amount that is not a number. The rule then counts as failed.
Rule ids starting with SUM- are Summand's own checks. Each is described with cause and fix in the error code catalogue:
Id | Meaning

SUM-XML | The XML is not well-formed SUM-XSD | The XML does not match the UBL or CII XML Schema (unexpected, missing, misplaced or repeated element, attribute, or value format) SUM-FORMAT | Not a UBL or CII invoice, or ZUGFeRD 1.0 SUM-PDF | The PDF cannot be read or has no embedded invoice SUM-PROFILE | MINIMUM or BASIC WL (error), or an unknown specification identifier (warning) SUM-EXTENDED | Info that EXTENDED violations were reported as warnings SUM-PDF-LEVEL | The PDF metadata declares a different profile than the XML SUM-LEITWEG | The buyer reference looks like a Leitweg-ID but its check digits are wrong SUM-RULESET | ruleSets names a rule set or version that is not bundled (error; no rule set runs)
Exit codes on the command line

summand validate reports the verdict in its exit code: 0 when every invoice is valid, 1 when at least one is invalid, which includes input that is not an invoice (SUM-FORMAT, SUM-XML, SUM-PDF), and 2 when the command could not run, for example because a file does not exist. See CLI.
Errors in rules and the engine

Schema errors and Schematron errors are reported together: like the KoSIT validator, Summand keeps running the rules when the schema check fails, so you see every problem at once. The schema errors come first in errors.
If a rule fires where you think it should not, compare with the KoSIT validator and open an issue with the invoice (anonymised). The bundled rule sets are listed in Rule sets.

Summand checks incoming e-invoices in TypeScript. It reads XRechnung, ZUGFeRD and Factur-X invoices, as UBL or UN/CEFACT CII XML or as a PDF with the XML embedded, and validates them against EN 16931 and the German XRechnung rules. It runs in Node.js, in serverless functions and in the browser. No Java, no external service, nothing leaves your machine.
Since 1 January 2025 every business in Germany has to be able to receive e-invoices, and creating them is a solved problem (libraries such as node-zugferd do it well). Checking what arrives is not: the reference validator of KoSIT is a Java application with Xerces, Saxon and XSLT. Summand brings the same checks to JavaScript: the XML Schema first, then the Schematron rules.

The official rules, not a re-implementation. Summand ships the Schematron rules published by CEN/TC 434 (EN 16931 validation artefacts 1.3.16) and by KoSIT (XRechnung Schematron 2.6.0 for XRechnung 3.0) and runs them with its own XPath 2.0 and Schematron engine. XML Schema validation: the document is checked against the official UBL 2.1 or UN/CEFACT CII D16B schema first, as the KoSIT validator does. Misspelt, missing, misplaced or repeated elements, unknown attributes and malformed dates or numbers are reported with the id SUM-XSD. See XML Schema. UBL and CII: UBL 2.1 Invoice and CreditNote, UN/CEFACT Cross Industry Invoice D16B. PDF: extracts factur-x.xml, zugferd-invoice.xml or xrechnung.xml from a ZUGFeRD / Factur-X PDF and compares the profile with the PDF's XMP metadata. Profiles: recognises XRechnung 3.0 (standard, extension, CVD), EN 16931, Factur-X BASIC, EXTENDED, BASIC WL and MINIMUM, Peppol BIS Billing 3.0, and picks the right rules. The severity changes of the KoSIT configuration for XRechnung are applied as well.

Clear results: every message has the rule id (BR-CO-10, BR-DE-15), the severity, the XPath and the line in the XML, plus a summary of the invoice (number, date, parties, totals). Leitweg-ID check for invoices to German public buyers. CLI for scripts and CI: summand validate invoices/*.pdf. No dependencies. About 135 KB gzipped including all rule sets, schemas and both languages.
How close is it to the official validator?

The test suite runs the official test material on every change:
Test material | Result
CEN EN 16931 unit tests (1,142 expectations for UBL Invoice, UBL Credit Note and CII) | all pass KoSIT XRechnung test suite (reference invoices, UBL and CII, standard, extension, CVD) | all valid (schema and rules) XML Schema check compared with Xerces (the schema validator the KoSIT validator uses) on the test material and about 2,800 modified invoices | same verdict for every document CEN example invoices (UBL and CII) | all valid

Be clear about this when you build on it:
Signatures and extension content. The content of UBL extensions (ext:ExtensionContent) is validated laxly, as the schema says, but the UBL signature schemas are not bundled, so a sig:UBLDocumentSignatures block is not checked. See XML Schema for the details. Not the reference implementation. For disputes, the KoSIT validator with the official configuration is authoritative. Summand aims to give the same result and is tested against the same material, but it is not certified. No Peppol BIS rules (PEPPOL-EN16931-R…) and no dedicated Factur-X EXTENDED rules yet. EXTENDED invoices are checked against EN 16931, with violations reported as warnings by default. No PDF/A check. Summand reads the embedded XML; whether the PDF itself is valid PDF/A-3 is not checked. No legal advice. A valid invoice under EN 16931 can still be wrong in content (wrong VAT rate, wrong buyer).
Summand Pro adds a readable invoice view with the validation report for inboxes and accounting, and batch validation with reports, duplicate detection and an audit trail.

Every message of a validation has an id. Ids that look like BR-CO-10, BR-DE-15 or UBL-CR-646 are rules of the bundled rule sets, see Rule sets. Ids that start with SUM- are Summand's own checks and are listed here. They are part of the stable API: a code is never renamed or reused for something else within a major version, and new codes only appear in minor releases. SUM-DEPRECATED (1.1) was removed in 2.0.0 together with the option it reported; nothing emits it any more and the code will not be reused.
The same codes are reported in English and German (lang: "de"); only the message text changes. Match on id, never on the text.
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Every finding in result.errors, result.warnings and result.infos has these fields, always set and with these types:
Field | Type | Contract
id | string | The stable code: a rule id of a bundled rule set (BR-CO-10, BR-DE-15, UBL-CR-646, ...) or a SUM- code from the table below. Rule ids are the upstream's; SUM- codes are never renamed or reused. severity | "error" \ | "warning" \ | "info" | Always equal to the list the message is in (errors has only "error", and so on), so a message is self-describing once you copy it out of the result. ruleSet | RuleSetId \ | "summand" | Which rule set produced it: en16931-ubl, en16931-cii, xrechnung-ubl, xrechnung-cii, or summand for the SUM- codes. A message with a SUM- id has ruleSet: "summand" and a message from a rule set never has an id starting with SUM-. message | string | Text for people. Not stable; do not match on it.
The field is called id, as in 1.x; it was not renamed to code. location, line and evaluationError are optional. The same fields are in the --json output of the CLI. A test checks the contract above on real results.
Code | Severity | Raised when
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

SUM-XML | error | The XML is not well-formed SUM-FORMAT | error | Not a UBL or CII invoice, or ZUGFeRD 1.0 SUM-PDF | error | The PDF cannot be read or has no embedded invoice SUM-XSD | error | The XML does not match the UBL or CII XML Schema SUM-PROFILE | error or warning | MINIMUM or BASIC WL profile (error), unknown or missing specification identifier (warning) SUM-EXTENDED | info | EXTENDED violations were reported as warnings SUM-LEITWEG | warning | The Leitweg-ID has wrong check digits SUM-PDF-LEVEL | warning | The PDF metadata declares a different profile than the XML SUM-RULESET | error | ruleSets names a rule set or version that is not bundled, or the removed xrechnung option is passed SUM-BATCH | error | validateMany could not process an input (not a verdict about the invoice)
When validation stops early (SUM-XML, SUM-FORMAT, SUM-PDF, SUM-RULESET), the result has that one error and no syntax, profile, summary or schemas. SUM-RULESET does not depend on the document: it is reported for every input, before the document is read.
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Severity: error. Fields: line of the problem; no location. Validation stops.
Meaning. The input is not well-formed XML, so nothing else can be checked.
Causes. A truncated or corrupted file; an unescaped & or < in text; a tag that is not closed or closed in the wrong order; more than one root element; text before the XML declaration; a file saved in an encoding other than the one the declaration states. A PDF handed over as a string (not as bytes) also ends up here, because strings are always treated as XML.
Fix. Open the file at the reported line. Escape & as &, close every tag, and make the encoding of the XML declaration match the file. Pass PDFs as Uint8Array or ArrayBuffer, not as text.
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Severity: error. No line, no location. Validation stops.
Meaning. The XML is well-formed but is not an invoice Summand can validate: the root element is none of UBL Invoice, UBL CreditNote or UN/CEFACT CrossIndustryInvoice (in the right namespace), or it is ZUGFeRD 1.0 (urn:ferd:CrossIndustryDocument:invoice:1p0), which is not supported and does not comply with EN 16931.
Causes. Another document type (order, despatch advice, application response), an XML wrapper around the invoice, a wrong or missing namespace, or an invoice in the ZUGFeRD 1.0 format.
Fix. Pass the invoice document itself. For UBL use the Invoice-2 or CreditNote-2 namespace, for CII the CrossIndustryInvoice:100 namespace. Re-issue ZUGFeRD 1.0 invoices as ZUGFeRD 2.x / Factur-X or XRechnung.
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Severity: error. No line, no location. Validation stops.
Meaning. The bytes are a PDF, but no invoice XML could be taken from it: it contains no embedded invoice XML (the usual case), or the PDF could not be read at all.
Causes. A plain PDF that is a rendering of an invoice only; a PDF/A-3 without the associated file; an encrypted PDF or one whose embedded file uses a stream encoding Summand does not read (readPdf().encrypted tells the first); a damaged file.
Fix. Create the PDF with an e-invoice tool that embeds the XML as factur-x.xml (or zugferd-invoice.xml, xrechnung.xml), or send the XML itself. Check with summand extract invoice.pdf.
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Severity: error. Fields: location (XPath) and line. Validation continues, so the Schematron rules run as well and schema errors come first in errors.
Meaning. The XML does not match the XML Schema of its syntax (OASIS UBL 2.1, or UN/CEFACT CII D16B). The message names the element or attribute. The kind of violation is one of SchemaFindingKind (visible with validateSchema):
Kind | Meaning
unexpected-element | An element that is not allowed at this place (also an undeclared root element) missing-element | A required element is missing element-order | Elements are in the wrong order too-many | An element occurs more often than allowed content | Text or child elements where the type allows none, or the reverse missing-attribute | A required attribute is missing unknown-attribute | An attribute that is not declared attribute-value | An attribute value is invalid or differs from the fixed value value | The text does not match its type or facets (date, decimal, length, pattern, code)
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Causes. Elements in the wrong order (the schemas are strict about sequence), a date that is not YYYY-MM-DD, an amount with a thousands separator or comma, a missing currencyID, an element from another syntax, or a text value that is too long.
Fix. Correct the element at location. Fix order and format problems first; many Schematron errors are follow-on effects of a broken structure. Do not switch the schema check off to hide them (schema: false / --no-schema): the KoSIT validator reports them too.
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Severity: error (MINIMUM, BASIC WL) or warning (unknown or missing identifier). No line, no location.
Meaning, error. The invoice declares the ZUGFeRD / Factur-X MINIMUM or BASIC WL profile. They omit information EN 16931 requires (for example invoice lines), so they are not e-invoices under EN 16931 and, in Germany, not under § 14 UStG. No rule sets run for them in "auto" mode.
Meaning, warning. The specification identifier (BT-24) is missing or not one Summand knows. The invoice is validated against EN 16931 only, so XRechnung-specific rules (BR-DE-*) are not applied.
Causes. An invoice created with a reduced profile, an invoice generator that does not write BT-24, or a typo in the identifier.
Fix. Issue the invoice in the EN 16931 (COMFORT), BASIC, EXTENDED or XRechnung profile. For the warning, set BT-24 (cbc:CustomizationID in UBL, ram:GuidelineSpecifiedDocumentContextParameter/ram:ID in CII) to the identifier of the profile you intend, for example urn:cen.eu:en16931:2017#compliant#urn:xeinkauf.de:kosit:xrechnung_3.0. To apply the XRechnung rules to an invoice that does not declare XRechnung, use ruleSets: ["en16931", "xrechnung"] / --rule-sets en16931,xrechnung. See Profiles.
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Severity: info. No line, no location.
Meaning. The invoice is ZUGFeRD / Factur-X EXTENDED, which may contain information beyond EN 16931. In the default extended: "lenient" mode, violations of EN 16931 rules are reported as warnings instead of errors, and this message tells you so. It is not a problem with the invoice.
Fix. Nothing to fix. To treat EN 16931 violations as errors, use extended: "strict" / --strict-extended; the info is then not reported.
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Severity: warning. No line, no location. Only reported when the option leitwegId is not false (CLI: without --no-leitweg).
Meaning. The buyer reference (BT-10) has the shape of a Leitweg-ID (for example 04011000-1234512345-06) but its two check digits are wrong. German public buyers reject invoices with an unknown Leitweg-ID.
Causes. A typo, a Leitweg-ID copied without its check digits, or a made-up value in a test invoice.
Fix. Use the Leitweg-ID the buyer published, exactly. summand leitweg prints the correct check digits for the address part. If BT-10 is a purchase order number that merely looks like a Leitweg-ID, set leitwegId: false.
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Severity: warning. No line, no location.
Meaning. The conformance level in the PDF's XMP metadata (for example EN 16931) differs from the profile of the embedded XML (for example BASIC). Readers that trust the metadata will treat the invoice differently than the XML says.
Causes. The XML was replaced or regenerated without updating the PDF metadata, or the metadata was written for another profile.
Fix. Regenerate the PDF so the XMP ConformanceLevel matches the profile in the XML (BT-24).
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Severity: error. No line, no location. Validation stops before the document is read.
Meaning. An entry of the ruleSets option (CLI: --rule-sets) is not a bundled rule set, or names a version that is not bundled. The message lists what is known. No rule set ran, so the result says nothing about the invoice.
Causes. The removed xrechnung option is still passed (removed in 2.0.0, use ruleSets), a typo ("xrechung"), a version that was never bundled or was removed ("xrechnung@2.4.0"), a version of another rule set ("en16931@2.6.0"), an empty version ("xrechnung@"), or a config file written for a newer Summand version than the installed one.
Fix. Use en16931 or xrechnung, optionally with @ and one of the versions ruleSetInfo({ versions: "all" }) (CLI: summand rules) lists. See Rule sets and versions. The CLI treats the same mistake as a usage error (exit code 2) before it reads any file.
The shape of a message (2.0 contract)

Severity: error. Appears as BatchResult.error ({ code, message }), not inside a ValidationResult, because there is no result.
Meaning. validateMany could not process one input: the file could not be read, the input could not be sent to the worker thread, or the worker thread failed. This is different from an invalid invoice, which is a normal result with valid: false. The other inputs of the batch are not affected.
Causes. A path that does not exist or is a directory, no permission, a data value that is not text or bytes, a worker that ran out of memory or exited, or a batch that was stopped.
Fix. Read error.message (it carries the operating system error for files). Check paths and permissions. For very large invoices, validate them with concurrency: 1 or a smaller batch. A failed input never stops the batch; collect the entries with error and report them like the CLI does for unreadable files (exit code 2).

A message from a rule set can have evaluationError: the rule could not be evaluated, for example because an amount is not a number. The rule then counts as failed. This is not a SUM- code. Usually a SUM-XSD error for the same element tells you what is wrong.
Exit codes of the summand command

Code | Meaning
0 | Success. Every invoice given to validate is valid (warnings do not count unless --warnings-as-errors), or the command did what was asked (extract, leitweg, rules, --help, --version). rules --check without --fail-on-outdated also exits 0 when newer releases exist or the sources cannot be reached. 1 | Findings. At least one invoice is invalid, or has warnings with --warnings-as-errors; this includes input that is not an invoice at all (SUM-FORMAT, SUM-XML). Also leitweg with an invalid ID. 2 | The command could not run: unknown command or flag, missing arguments, a file that cannot be read, extract on a file that is not a PDF or has no embedded XML, no command at all (help is printed), or an internal failure. No verdict was produced for the files that were not read. 3 | summand rules --check --fail-on-outdated found a newer upstream release of a bundled rule set.
Exit codes of the summand command

The split is the same as in ESLint: 1 means the check ran and found problems, 2 means it could not run. With several files, validate still validates the readable ones when one path fails; the exit code is then 2, even if another file was invalid. A script that only needs pass or fail can test for non-zero; to tell the two apart, test for 1 and 2, or use --json and read valid.
With --json, validate prints one line per file: the object { "file": " ", ...ValidationResult }. The fields are part of the stable API.

The first four rows are the default versions. Select a version with ruleSets, for example ["en16931", "xrechnung@2.5.0"], see Rule sets and versions. The names en16931 and xrechnung stand for the UBL or CII id of the same row, by the syntax of the invoice.

New releases of the rule sets come out a few times a year. Summand publishes a minor version for each, with the change in the changelog. summand rules lists the bundled versions and summand rules --check asks whether newer releases exist, see Rule sets and versions.

Accessibility checks for CI and tests, client-ready reports and accessibility statements in five languages. Built on axe-core, no overlay.
Surjection helps agencies make accessibility part of every project instead of a one-off scan. It runs axe-core in Playwright and Vitest, maps every finding to WCAG 2.2 and EN 301 549, and fails the build only on new problems thanks to a baseline for existing sites.
It also generates the accessibility statement (Erklärung zur Barrierefreiheit) in German, Swiss German, French, Italian and English, and ships small accessible React building blocks. Surjection is deliberately not an overlay widget: it helps you fix the code, it does not hide problems. Automated tests find only part of all barriers, so Surjection does not promise legal conformity.

Yes. The documented API, the command line options, the config file, the formats of the results, baseline and checklist files and the ids of Surjection's own rules follow semantic versioning, and the Pro packages share the version. Within 2.x nothing of that is removed. What can change in any release: which problems the checks find, because axe-core is updated and finds more, and the texts of reports. Version 1.x gets security and bug fixes for 12 months after the release of 2.0.0. The stability page in the docs lists both.
Does Surjection make my website legally compliant?
No tool can promise that. Automated tests detect only part of all barriers. Surjection makes testing and documentation part of your workflow, but a manual review is still needed.
No. Overlays add a widget on top of a site and leave the code unchanged. Surjection runs in development and CI and helps you fix the code itself.

Who issues the invoice, and is VAT included?
Polar sells Surjection Pro as merchant of record. It handles checkout, invoices and VAT for your country.
Can I use the open-source part on its own?

Install the package and Playwright with a browser:
pnpm add -D @sweberdev/surjection @playwright/test pnpm exec playwright install chromium
With npm: npm i -D @sweberdev/surjection @playwright/test and npx playwright install chromium.
Check a page:
npx surjection check https://example.ch --locale de
Each page prints one line. The command exits with code 1 when issues remain.
Write a report you can attach to a pull request or hand to your team:
npx surjection check https://example.ch --out-md a11y.md --out-json a11y.json
Run it on every build. See GitHub Actions, or use the Playwright helper in your existing end-to-end tests.
Node.js 20 or newer Playwright 1.40 or newer for page checks (@playwright/test or playwright) Vitest 3 or newer for the component matcher (types target Vitest 5)

A site you take over may have hundreds of issues. Fixing them takes time, but new ones should not be added meanwhile. A baseline records the current findings so the build fails only on new ones.
# Record the current state once and commit the file npx surjection check --config surjection.config.json --update-baseline git add surjection-baseline.json
# Every later run ignores what is in the baseline npx surjection check --config surjection.config.json
Each entry records the page path, the rule and the element selector, plus the stable id the finding has in the results file:
{ "id": "3f2a9c01b7de", "page": "/shop", "rule": "image-alt", "target": "#hero", "note": "Ticket SHOP-214" }
Host and protocol are ignored, so the same baseline works for localhost, preview and production. The optional note is yours: write down why an entry is accepted or which ticket tracks it. It survives --update-baseline as long as the finding stays.
A baseline written by Surjection 1.x (a list of "/shop | image-alt | #hero" strings) is still read. Convert it once with surjection convert surjection-baseline.json --out surjection-baseline.json.
npx surjection check [urls...] [options] npx surjection statement --config statement.json --out erklaerung.md npx surjection init --base-url https://example.ch --sitemap

surjection init writes a surjection.config.json and a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/accessibility.yml) that checks every pull request and runs once a week. Existing files are never overwritten. --no-workflow skips the workflow, --project sets the project name.

Pass absolute URLs, paths with --base-url, or a sitemap:
npx surjection check --base-url https://preview.example.ch / /shop /kontakt npx surjection check --sitemap https://example.ch/sitemap.xml --max-pages 100
Sitemap indexes are followed one level deep. --max-pages (default 50) keeps large shops manageable.

Code | Meaning
0 | No failing issues 1 | Issues remain after baseline and --fail-on 2 | Usage or runtime error, e.g. Playwright missing, or pages that could not be loaded. The other pages are still checked and written to the reports
The CLI starts Chromium through Playwright. Set SURJECTIONCHROMIUMPATH to use a browser that is already installed.

@sweberdev/surjection/component checks one component instead of a whole page. It runs in the browser, in jsdom and in happy-dom, and needs no Playwright. Rules about whole pages (landmarks, a single h1) are switched off.

jsdom has no layout engine, so colour contrast and target size cannot be decided there; axe-core skips them or reports them as "needs review". Run the same stories in a real browser (Storybook test runner) to include them. Keyboard and reflow checks need a page and stay in surjection check.

A green run does not mean a site is accessible. Automatic tests can decide only part of the criteria. surjection coverage shows the split for the 55 success criteria of WCAG 2.2 at levels A and AA:
npx surjection coverage            # table as Markdown npx surjection coverage --json     # for scripts npx surjection coverage --out coverage.md
Class | Meaning
mostly automatic | The rules cover the core of the criterion. A finding is almost always right, a pass says a lot, but not everything. partly automatic | Rules find missing or wrong markup, a person must judge the rest (for example whether alternative text describes the image). manual only | No automatic test. Needs a person.
The table lists the rules behind every criterion. They are read from the installed axe-core version and Surjection's own checks (--keyboard, --layout), so the list follows the tool when axe-core is updated. Which criteria count as "mostly" is our own judgement and can change between minor versions, see Stability.
Use the table to plan manual testing: the Pro checklist covers all 55 criteria, with the automatic ones pre-marked by the last run.
A passing run is no proof of conformance, not even for the criteria marked "mostly automatic".

Steps are the same as for states: click, hover, fill, press, waitFor and wait. A flow without a check step is checked once at the end, labelled end. Labels and flow names contain no spaces or #. If a step fails, the run stops with the flow and step named, for example Flow "checkout", step "click #to-address" failed: .... The baseline keeps every check of a flow apart, so you can accept the findings of one step and keep failing on the others.
A flow follows one path. It does not click through all alternatives; for that write Playwright tests and call expectAccessible(page) where you want to check. Flows can be combined with urls and states in the same config.

The CLI adds its Markdown report to the job summary when it runs in GitHub Actions. npx surjection init writes a ready workflow and config file for you. This workflow checks a preview deployment on every pull request:
name: Accessibility
on: pull_request
jobs: a11y: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 - run: npm ci - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium - run: npx surjection check --config surjection.config.json --out-json a11y.json - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 if: always() with: name: accessibility path: a11y.json
{ "baseUrl": "https://preview.example.ch", "urls": ["/", "/shop", "/checkout", "/kontakt"], "failOn": "serious", "locale": "de-CH", "project": "Muster AG" }
To check the app built in the same job, start it in the background first, e.g. npm run build && npm start &, and point baseUrl at http://localhost:3000.
Commit surjection-baseline.json next to the config when you use a baseline.

--out-junit a11y.xml writes a JUnit report that these systems show as test results, one failed test per rule and page. In GitLab:
accessibility: image: node:22 script: - npm i -g @sweberdev/surjection @playwright/test - npx playwright install --with-deps chromium - surjection check --config surjection.config.json --out-junit a11y.xml artifacts: when: always reports: junit: a11y.xml

axe-core looks at the page as it is. Two common barriers only show up when someone actually uses the keyboard, so Surjection can also press Tab through each page.
npx surjection check --base-url https://preview.example.ch / /shop --keyboard
In a config file: "keyboard": true. In Playwright tests: expectAccessible(page, { keyboard: true }), or call checkKeyboard(page) from @sweberdev/surjection/playwright on its own.
The keyboard findings work like all others: they appear in every report, count for --fail-on and can be accepted in the baseline.

Rule surjection-focus-trap, WCAG 2.1.2 (A), EN 301 549 9.2.1.2, impact critical.
Surjection presses Tab up to the number of focusable elements plus ten. If focus keeps cycling through the same few elements and never reaches the rest of the page, that is a trap. Typical causes are dialogs that hold focus after they should have closed, embedded players and chat widgets. The finding lists the elements of the cycle.
A dialog that is open on purpose may hold focus as long as Escape closes it. Check such a case by hand and accept it in the baseline.

Rule surjection-focus-visible, WCAG 2.4.7 (AA), EN 301 549 9.2.4.7, impact serious.
For every element that receives focus, Surjection compares outline, shadow, border, background, text colour and underline with and without focus. If nothing changes, keyboard users cannot see where they are. Usually outline: none without a replacement is the cause:
a:focus-visible, button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #0b6e4f; outline-offset: 2px; }
A change elsewhere, for example on a parent element, is not detected and leads to a false positive. Accept it in the baseline after checking it by hand.

Rule surjection-focus-order, WCAG 2.4.3 (A), EN 301 549 9.2.4.3, impact moderate.
While pressing Tab, Surjection notes where each focused element sits. If focus jumps up by more than 200 px, for example because of positive tabindex values or content moved with CSS, the finding lists the affected elements (at most ten). Fixed and sticky elements such as headers are ignored. A sensible order is more than this rule can judge, so treat the finding as a pointer: remove positive tabindex values and keep the DOM order the same as the visual order.

Save a logged-in session once with Playwright and pass it to the check:
npx playwright codegen --save-storage=auth.json https://preview.example.ch/login npx surjection check --storage-state auth.json /konto /bestellungen
auth.json holds session cookies. Keep it out of the repository; in CI create it in a setup step or store it as a secret. In a config file: "storageState": "auth.json".

The keyboard check covers traps and visible focus. Whether the focus order really makes sense, whether all functions work with the keyboard and whether shortcuts can be turned off still needs a manual test, see the Pro checklist.

Two WCAG criteria depend on a changed window or changed styles, so axe-core cannot decide them. --layout tests both and reports them like all other findings.
npx surjection check --base-url https://preview.example.ch / /shop --layout
In a config file: "layout": true. In Playwright tests: expectAccessible(page, { layout: true }), or call checkLayout(page) from @sweberdev/surjection/playwright. The page is changed during the check and restored afterwards.

Rule surjection-reflow, WCAG 1.4.10 (AA), EN 301 549 9.1.4.10, impact serious.
The window is set to 320 CSS pixels, which is a 1280 pixel window at 400 % zoom. The page must not need sideways scrolling. Surjection lists the elements that reach beyond the right edge, the cause and not every child of it. Content that scrolls inside its own box, such as a wide table in a container with overflow-x: auto, is allowed by the criterion and not reported. Fixed elements are ignored.
Typical fixes are fixed pixel widths on containers, images and embeds without max-width: 100%, and long unbreakable strings such as URLs (overflow-wrap: anywhere).

Rule surjection-text-spacing, WCAG 1.4.12 (AA), EN 301 549 9.1.4.12, impact serious.
Surjection applies the values of the criterion: line height 1.5, letter spacing 0.12 em, word spacing 0.16 em and paragraph spacing 2 em. Elements that cut off text with the new spacing but did not before are reported. Fixed heights combined with overflow: hidden on buttons, cards and menu items are the usual cause: use min-height instead.
Two-dimensional content such as maps, data tables, diagrams and toolbars may scroll in two directions. If such content makes the page fail, exclude it with --exclude and test it by hand.

Surjection 2.0 changes the results format, raises the minimum Node version and adds flows, a coverage table and component checks. Most projects only need to upgrade Node and, if they use the results file in their own scripts, read one new version number.
pnpm add -D @sweberdev/surjection@^2.0.0

Node 22 or newer. Node 20 is end of life. Set node-version: 22 in your CI (the workflow written by surjection init already does). Results file version: 2. --out-json writes version 2: tool, run and an id per affected element are new, nothing was removed. If your own scripts check version === 1, accept 2 as well. Surjection itself, --compare-with and the Pro history read both versions. Convert old files with surjection convert old.json --out new.json, see Results format. Baseline version: 2. --update-baseline writes entries with id, page, rule, target and an optional note. A baseline of version 1 is still read, so nothing breaks if you do not touch it. Run surjection convert surjection-baseline.json --out surjection-baseline.json once to switch and commit the result. fingerprints(page) returns ids. The exported function now returns the 12 character ids instead of " | | " strings. Only code that reads these strings itself is affected. createBaseline and applyBaseline take a version 2 baseline; use normalizeBaseline(json) to read any version. ResultsFile type. version is 2, tool is required. Code that builds a results file by hand should use createResults(pages).
Nothing else was removed. Surjection 1.x had no deprecated exports.

Flows: check a journey, with a check after each step. Coverage: surjection coverage shows which of the 55 WCAG 2.2 A/AA criteria are tested automatically. Component checks: @sweberdev/surjection/component for Storybook and Testing Library. Results format: stable ids per finding, run settings and tool version. Config: flows is new, everything else stays as it was (states is not deprecated). The JSON schema knows flows.

Pro 2.0 adds the WCAG-EM conformance report, the ACR export and the re-test flow, see the Pro pages. Pro 1.0.1 and newer read results of version 2; if you run an older Pro version, update it before you update Surjection, or convert the file.
Version 1.x gets security and bug fixes for 12 months after 2.0.0. See Stability.

expectAccessible(page, options) and checkPage(page, options) accept:
Option | Meaning
standard | wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21aa, wcag22aa (default) bestPractice | Also run axe-core best-practice rules disableRules | Rule ids to skip include / exclude | CSS selectors to limit or skip parts of the page locale | Language of messages failOn | Lowest impact that fails (only expectAccessible) baseline | Accepted findings (only expectAccessible)
checkPage returns the normalized result without failing, e.g. to build your own report.
Only the main frame is checked. Content inside iframes, such as embedded maps or payment forms, needs its own check.

The first focusable element on the page. It lets keyboard users jump past the navigation (WCAG 2.4.1) and moves focus into the main content.
import { SkipLink } from "@sweberdev/surjection-react";
<SkipLink targetId="main" className="skip-link">Zum Inhalt springen</SkipLink> <Header /> <main id="main">…</main>
It stays hidden until it receives focus. Style the visible state through className.

Text for screen readers that is not shown on screen, e.g. for icon buttons:
<button type="button"> <CloseIcon aria-hidden="true" /> <VisuallyHidden>Schliessen</VisuallyHidden> </button>

true when the user asked the system to reduce motion. Use it to turn off parallax, auto-playing carousels and large transitions.
const reduce = useReducedMotion(); <motion.div animate={{ x: 100 }} transition={{ duration: reduce ? 0 : 0.4 }} />

If you work through the manual checklist of Surjection Pro, the statement can be derived from it. Leave status out of statement.json and pass the checklist:
npx surjection statement --config statement.json --checklist checklist.json --out erklaerung.html
Status follows from the decisions (no failed criterion: full, some: partial, none passed: none), every failed criterion becomes a known issue with its note and planned fix date, and the date of the last test becomes lastReviewedOn. Known issues you list in statement.json stay and are not duplicated. While criteria are still untested the command stops with an error, because a statement must not claim more than was checked.

Field | Meaning
locale | de, de-CH (uses "ss" instead of "ß"), fr, it, en status | full, partial or none standard | Default WCAG 2.2 AA / EN 301 549 V3.2.1 knownIssues | What is not accessible, why, the alternative and the planned fix date method | self or third-party (with auditor) contact | Email, optional phone and postal address for feedback enforcement | The authority people can turn to. Presets: enforcementBodies.DE, enforcementBodies.AT
The text is a starting point, not legal advice. Check the requirements for your service and have the statement reviewed before you publish it. Surjection Pro fills status and knownIssues from your manual checklist.

Step | Meaning
{ "click": " " } | Click an element { "hover": " " } | Move the mouse over an element { "fill": [" ", " "] } | Type into a field { "press": " " } | Press a key, e.g. Enter or Escape { "waitFor": " " } | Wait until an element appears { "wait": 500 } | Wait in milliseconds (at most 10000)
Every step waits up to five seconds. If one fails, the check stops with the state and step named, for example State "menu-open", step "click #menu" failed: ..., so a changed page is not mistaken for an accessible one.
For journeys over several pages or steps, with a check after each step, see Flows. For anything more complicated use Playwright: navigate in your test and call expectAccessible(page) at the point you want to check.

Version 1.0.0 adds no breaking change compared with 0.9. If you run 0.9 you can upgrade without touching anything.
pnpm add -D @sweberdev/surjection@^1.0.0

Nothing was removed on the way to 1.0, but defaults and checks grew. Look at these points:
Since | What to know
0.3 | --keyboard checks focus traps and visible focus. Opt-in. 0.4 | --screenshots stores a PNG of each affected element. Opt-in. 0.5 | --layout tests reflow and text spacing. Opt-in. 0.6 | states in the config and the focus-order rule (inside --keyboard). Accepted keyboard findings in a baseline do not cover the new rule, so it can show up once. 0.7 | --out-sarif, --color-scheme, --reduced-motion, and $schema in the config. Opt-in. 0.8 | --compare-with for before and after images. Opt-in. 0.9 | --concurrency, surjection statement --checklist. Pages that cannot be loaded no longer stop the run: the others are checked, and the exit code is 2.
If CI treated a failed page load as a crash before, it still fails (exit code 2), but now with results for all other pages.

axe-core is updated with Surjection. A newer version may find issues that were not reported before. Run surjection check --update-baseline once if you want to accept the current state and fail only on new problems, see Baseline.
Update @weber-development/surjection-report, -history and -checklist to 1.0.0 together. Existing history folders and checklist files keep working.

Since June 2025 the European Accessibility Act applies to many online shops and digital services, in Germany through the Barrierefreiheitsstärkungsgesetz (BFSG). Agencies have to build accessible sites and show what they did. A one-off scan before launch does not help much: the next release can break it again.
Surjection makes accessibility part of the normal workflow:
Checks in development and CI. Playwright, Vitest and a CLI on top of axe-core, the most widely used accessibility engine. Findings you can act on. Each one names the affected elements, the WCAG 2.2 success criterion and the EN 301 549 clause, in German, Swiss German, French, Italian or English. A baseline. Existing problems on a site you took over do not block every build. New ones do. Documentation. A Markdown report for pull requests, a JSON file for further processing, and a generator for the accessibility statement. Accessible building blocks for React. Skip link, visually hidden text, live announcements and reduced motion.

Overlay widgets put a toolbar on top of a site and leave the code unchanged. They do not fix missing labels, broken focus order or unclear structure, and many people who rely on assistive technology find them in the way. Surjection works the other way round: it shows developers what to fix in the code.

Automated tests detect only part of all barriers. They cannot judge whether alternative text is meaningful, whether the focus order makes sense or whether a video has correct captions. Surjection therefore lists rules it could not decide as "needs manual review", and Surjection Pro adds a guided checklist for the criteria that need a person.
A passing run is not proof of conformance with WCAG, EN 301 549, the BFSG or any other law. See Legal notes.

Package | License | Content
@sweberdev/surjection | MIT | Checks, CLI, baseline, reports, statement generator @sweberdev/surjection-react | MIT | Accessible React building blocks @weber-development/surjection-* | Commercial | Surjection Pro: branded client reports, history across projects, manual checklist

Surjection is a testing and documentation tool. It is not legal advice, and using it does not make a website or app compliant with WCAG, EN 301 549, the European Accessibility Act, the German BFSG, the Austrian BaFG, the Swiss BehiG or any other law.
Surjection does
run the automated rules of axe-core and map them to WCAG and EN 301 549, list rules it could not decide as "needs manual review", generate a structured accessibility statement from the data you provide.
Surjection does not
find all barriers. Automated tests cover only part of the success criteria, decide whether your service falls under a law, or which exemptions apply, review the content of the statement it generates.
You decide which pages and states to test, which findings to accept in a baseline, and what your statement says. Have accessibility and legal questions reviewed by a qualified person.

Automated rules find only part of the barriers. @weber-development/surjection-checklist guides the manual part: the 55 success criteria of WCAG 2.2 level A and AA, each with a short instruction in English, German, Swiss German, French and Italian (--locale en | de | de-CH | fr | it). The editor, the Markdown list and the client report follow the language.
npx surjection-checklist init --project "Muster AG" npx surjection-checklist apply --checklist checklist.json --results a11y.json npx surjection-checklist edit --checklist checklist.json --locale de --out checklist.html npx surjection-checklist status --checklist checklist.json

Command | What it does
init | Creates checklist.json for a project (--level A or AA, default AA) apply | Marks criteria with automated findings as failed. It never marks a criterion as passed, because automated rules cover only part of it edit | Writes a self-contained HTML page. Set each criterion to passed, failed or not applicable, add notes, then download the updated checklist.json status | Prints how many criteria are untested, passed, failed and not applicable retest | After a re-test: criteria that failed only because of automated findings and have none left go back to untested, with a note. A person confirms the fix by hand; automated tests never mark a criterion as passed. Criteria you failed yourself stay failed markdown | Writes the checklist as Markdown statement | Writes the conformance status and known issues for the accessibility statement
The editor saves your progress in the browser until you download the file. It works offline and sends nothing anywhere.

For every criterion the editor has a note, the name of the person who tested ("Tested by"), the date (set when you decide), evidence links or references (one per line: a ticket, a video, a file name) and screenshots as evidence (PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF, up to 400 KB each). Images are stored inside checklist.json, so the file stays self-contained. Reports show links and images next to each criterion; only https links are made clickable. The Markdown list and the Word report name the evidence.
Into the statement and the report

npx surjection-checklist statement --checklist checklist.json --locale de --out statement-fields.json
Merge the fields into your statement config and run surjection statement, or skip the merge and pass the checklist directly: surjection statement --config statement.json --checklist checklist.json --out erklaerung.html. Pass the checklist to the report with --checklist to include it as a section.
statement refuses to run while criteria are still untested. The status is "fully conformant" only when no criterion failed, and every failed criterion becomes a known issue (your note, or the criterion title). Whether the result holds remains your judgement as the tester.

@weber-development/surjection-history keeps every run per project and shows what changed.
npx surjection check --config surjection.config.json --out-json a11y.json npx surjection-history record --results a11y.json --dir .surjection-history npx surjection-history dashboard --dir .surjection-history --locale de --out dashboard.html npx surjection-history badge --project "Muster AG" --locale de --out badge.svg

Stores the run as / / .json and prints which elements were fixed and which are new since the previous run of the same project. The project name comes from the results (project in surjection.config.json) or from --project.
Recorded .surjection-history/muster-ag/2026-10-05T08-00-00-000Z.json Fixed: 4  New: 1  Unchanged: 12 + /kontakt|color-contrast|.footer a
Elements are matched by page path, rule and selector (the same fingerprint as the baseline), so a fixed issue and a new one with the same rule are told apart.

Writes one accessible HTML page with a row per project: latest status, change since the previous run and a trend line. Locales: de, de-CH, fr, it, en.
The page has a search field, a filter for projects that got worse since the last check and a sort order (name, most issues, biggest increase). The controls need JavaScript and are hidden without it; the table is complete either way.
Keep the history folder in a private repository or a shared drive. In CI, record after each check and publish the dashboard as a build artefact.

Writes a status badge as SVG: the open issues after the latest run, red for critical or serious, orange for moderate, dark yellow for minor and green when nothing was found. The badge has a text alternative and white text with at least 4.5:1 contrast.
npx surjection-history badge --project "Muster AG" --locale de --out badge.svg npx surjection-history badge --out-dir badges   # one <project-slug>.svg per project
Put it in a README, the client portal or a status page. Publish the badges after each recorded run, for example as part of the same CI job. In code: renderBadge(projectStatus(slug, runs), "de").

Compares the latest run of a project with the previous one and lists what got worse. The exit code is 1 when new issues at or above --fail-on (default minor) appeared, so a scheduled job can alert you.
npx surjection-history regressions --fail-on serious --locale de --out-md monitoring.md
Without --project all projects are checked. In GitHub Actions the Markdown is added to the job summary. This workflow checks a client site every night, records the run and fails (GitHub then sends the failure mail to the repository watchers) when a new serious issue appears:

name: Accessibility monitoring on: schedule: [{ cron: "17 3 * * *" }] workflow_dispatch: permissions: contents: write jobs: monitor: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 registry-url: https://npm.pkg.github.com scope: "@weber-development" - run: npm i -g @sweberdev/surjection @weber-development/surjection-history @playwright/test env: NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SURJECTION_PRO_TOKEN }} - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium - run: surjection check --config surjection.config.json --out-json a11y.json --baseline none.json || true - run: surjection-history record --results a11y.json - run: | git config user.name "a11y-monitor" && git config user.email "monitor@users.noreply.github.com" git add .surjection-history && git commit -m "Record accessibility run" && git push - run: surjection-history regressions --fail-on serious --out-md monitoring.md

npx surjection-history regressions --fail-on serious \ --webhook "$MONITORING_WEBHOOK" \ --mail-to team@agency.ch --mail-from monitoring@agency.ch
--webhook posts a short message with the new issues as JSON ({"text": …, "content": …}), which Slack, Mattermost, Discord and Microsoft Teams workflows accept. --mail-to sends the same message by SMTP; set SURJECTIONSMTPURL (for example smtps://user:password@mail.agency.ch:465). Both are only used when something got worse at or above --fail-on, so a quiet week sends nothing. Webhook URL and SMTP URL are secrets: keep them in your CI secrets, never in the repository. The webhook must use https. The exit code stays 1 when issues got worse, so the job still fails.
In code: notificationText(reports), sendWebhook(url, text) and sendMail({ … }).

From Pro 2.1 pr-comment compares the results of a base (for example production) with the results of a pull request (its preview) and comments what is new, so reviewers see the effect of a change where they review it:
surjection check --base-url https://www.example.ch --out-json base.json surjection check --base-url https://preview-123.example.ch --out-json head.json surjection-history pr-comment --base base.json --head head.json --fail-on serious
The comment lists the new issues (impact, page, issue, element, what to fix), counts fixed and unchanged ones and ends with the reminder that automated tests find only part of all barriers. Issues are matched by page path, rule and element, so the host does not matter. There is one comment per pull request: every push updates it instead of adding another. The command exits with 1 when new issues reach --fail-on, so the job can block the merge; the comment is posted either way.

It reads GITHUBTOKEN, GITHUBREPOSITORY and the pull request number from the GitHub Actions environment (or --repo and --pr), and the workflow needs pull-requests: write. A pull request from a fork has no write token: the comment is then skipped with a note, and the result still appears in the job summary. --dry-run prints the Markdown without posting, --out-md writes it to a file, --locale picks German, Swiss German, French, Italian or English.
surjection-history init-ci --pull-request writes a ready workflow, .github/workflows/accessibility-pr.yml. You set the repository variables A11YBASEURL and A11YPREVIEWURL and the secret SURJECTIONPROTOKEN (the token with read:packages from your purchase). Adapt the step "Preview URL" if your host passes the preview address another way.
Beta: posting and updating the comment is verified against the GitHub API. The workflow file itself has not been run in a customer repository yet; check the first run and report problems.

regressions already tells you what got worse since the previous run. Run on a schedule it needs one more thing: the history must survive between runs, because every CI job starts empty. surjection-history init-ci --monitor writes .github/workflows/accessibility-monitor.yml, which
restores the history from the branch surjection-history (created on the first run), checks the site and records the run, compares it with the previous run and notifies by webhook (Slack, Teams, Discord) or mail only when something got worse at or above serious, saves the history back to the branch and fails the job when something got worse.
Secrets: SURJECTIONPROTOKEN (required) and, to be notified, A11YWEBHOOK, or A11YMAILTO, A11YMAILFROM and SURJECTIONSMTP_URL. The config needs a project name, because the history is kept per project. The schedule is daily at 05:00 UTC; change the cron line. Scheduled workflows may start late and GitHub pauses them in repositories without activity for 60 days.

Beta: the steps were run against a local Git remote and the notifications use the tested webhook and mail code, but the workflow has not run on a real schedule yet and delivery to a real Slack or mail account is not verified.

After a fix you do not need to check the whole site again. retest builds a config with only the pages, states and flows that had findings, and merge puts the new results into the earlier ones:
npx surjection-history retest --config surjection.config.json --results a11y.json \ --out retest.config.json                      # --criteria 1.4.3,2.4.7 limits it to these criteria npx surjection check --config retest.config.json --out-json retest.json npx surjection-history merge --base a11y.json --update retest.json --out a11y.json
merge prints how many findings were fixed, remain or are new in the re-tested pages. Pages that were not re-tested stay as they were, with their old test date, so the merged file is a complete results file for reports and the checklist. Pages that cannot be checked again from the config, for example a state you removed, are listed as skipped. retest exits with 1 when nothing needs a re-test; merge exits with 1 when new findings appeared.
A re-test is a shortcut for the time between full checks. A change in one place can break another page, so run the full check regularly (for example nightly or before a report).

import { compareRuns, loadProject, projectStatus, renderDashboard } from "@weber-development/surjection-history";
const runs = loadProject(".surjection-history", "Muster AG"); const diff = compareRuns(runs.at(-2)?.results, runs.at(-1)!.results);
Plans and prices are on packages.sweber.dev/surjection. After cancelling a subscription, the versions you installed keep working; only updates and access to new versions end.

# 1. Automated check of the client site npx surjection check --config surjection.config.json --out-json a11y.json
# 2. Keep the run in the history npx surjection-history record --results a11y.json
# 3. Manual review: mark automated failures, then work through the rest in the browser npx surjection-checklist apply --checklist checklist.json --results a11y.json npx surjection-checklist edit --checklist checklist.json --locale de --out checklist.html
# 4. Report for the client npx surjection-report --results a11y.json --brand brand.json --checklist checklist.json \ --history-dir .surjection-history --locale de --out report.pdf
After a fix, re-check only what was affected and update the checklist (re-test); for a client who needs a statement of the evaluation, write the conformance report or ACR.
Caution: A report or checklist from Surjection documents a test. It does not certify conformance with WCAG, EN 301 549, the BFSG, the Swiss BehiG or any other law. See Legal notice.
@weber-development/surjection-report turns a check into a report you can send to a client.

Cover page with your logo, the client and the date Summary by impact (critical, serious, moderate, minor) The most frequent issues Change since the last check, when a history is available Overview by WCAG 2.2 criterion with the matching EN 301 549 clauses Findings per page with the affected elements and a hint how to fix them Rules that need a manual review Your manual checklist, when you pass one Method and limits of the test
The report is available in German (de), Swiss German spelling (de-CH), French, Italian and English. The HTML report passes its own accessibility check.

npx surjection check --config surjection.config.json --out-json a11y.json npx surjection-report --results a11y.json --brand brand.json --client "Muster AG" --locale de --out report.pdf npx surjection-report --results a11y.json --locale de --out massnahmen.csv
Option | Meaning
--results | Output of surjection check --out-json --brand | Branding file, see below --client | Client name (default: the project name in the results) --client-url | Client website --checklist | Checklist file from surjection-checklist --history-dir | History folder from surjection-history, for trend and comparison --locale | de, de-CH, fr, it or en (default) --standard | Text for the target standard (default: WCAG 2.2 AA) --out | .html, .pdf, .docx or .csv

{ "agency": "Pixel & Co", "logo": "https://pixel.example/logo.png", "color": "#0055aa", "website": "https://pixel.example", "email": "hello@pixel.example", "phone": "+41 44 000 00 00" }
The logo can be a URL or a data: URL. A light brand colour is darkened automatically until text on it reaches a contrast of 4.5:1.

Run the check with --screenshots and the report shows a picture of every affected element next to its selector, so the client sees the problem instead of reading about it. The report stays one self-contained file.
npx surjection check --config surjection.config.json --out-json a11y.json --screenshots a11y-shots npx surjection-report --results a11y.json --brand brand.json --locale de --out report.pdf
The paths in a11y.json are resolved relative to the results file or the working directory. Elements inside iframes or shadow DOM and invisible elements get no picture.
Fixed since the last report (before and after)

Show the client what you fixed. Keep the results of the last run and pass them to the next one:
npx surjection check --config surjection.config.json --screenshots a11y-shots \ --compare-with last-a11y.json --out-json a11y.json npx surjection-report --results a11y.json --brand brand.json --client "Muster AG" --out report.pdf
Surjection copies the old screenshots aside before the run, takes new ones of the same elements and records each issue that is gone as fixed. The report gets the section "Fixed since the last report" with the image before and after for every item, in HTML, PDF and Word. An element that was removed from the page is listed without an after image. Many fixes are invisible (alt text, labels, lang): there both images look the same, and the list is the evidence. Contrast, size and layout fixes show best. Pages are matched by path, so a preview and the live site can be compared.

With --out report.docx you get the same content as an editable Word document, for clients who want to adjust texts or forward the report inside their organisation. The file uses real headings, table header rows, the document language and alt text for every element screenshot, so it is accessible itself. It needs no Playwright. In code: await renderDocx({ results, branding, client }).

With --out massnahmen.csv you get a fix list instead of a report: one row per affected element with page, rule, impact, WCAG and EN 301 549 criteria, selector and what to do, plus empty Status and Note columns for the team that fixes it. The file uses ; and a BOM, so Excel opens it directly with umlauts intact. Only --results and --locale are needed. In code: toFixListCsv(results, { locale: "de-CH" }).

From Pro 2.0 the same command writes two documents for clients who ask for a statement of the evaluation, not only a list of issues. Both need the checklist, because the outcome of each criterion is decided by a person:
npx surjection-report --results a11y.json --brand brand.json --checklist checklist.json \ --type conformance --locale de --out konformitaet.pdf
npx surjection-report --results a11y.json --brand brand.json --checklist checklist.json \ --type acr --product "Webshop" --product-version 4.2 --partial 1.4.3,2.4.7 --out acr.docx
Conformance report (--type conformance, .html, .pdf or .docx, in German, Swiss German, French, Italian and English) follows the steps of the W3C method WCAG-EM: scope (from the checklist), the sample of pages with date, the outcome per success criterion, the failed criteria with notes and planned fix, method and limits. The outcomes use the WCAG-EM terms:
Outcome | When

Passed | The checklist says "pass" and automated tests found nothing for the criterion Failed | The checklist says "fail", or automated tests found affected elements Inapplicable | The checklist says "not applicable" Cannot tell | Not decided yet, or the checklist and the automated tests disagree
Every row names the EN 301 549 clause, the basis (automated elements and pages, tester and date) and your remarks. If the checklist says "pass" but automated tests found affected elements, the criterion shows "cannot tell" and the report lists the conflict under "Points to resolve before publishing". Automated tests never mark a criterion as passed.

ACR (--type acr, English) is an Accessibility Conformance Report in the usual structure: product information, evaluation methods, terms and one table per level with the conformance levels Supports, Partially Supports, Does Not Support, Not Applicable and Not Evaluated. Failed criteria are reported as Does Not Support; list the ones that fail only in part with --partial. It is Surjection's own document, not a copy of the VPAT template, and not an official VPAT. If you use the name VPAT in your marketing, check the terms of the Information Technology Industry Council.
Both documents state that they confirm no legal conformity. The sample is the list of pages in the results: choosing a representative sample is the evaluator's job.

Clause 9 of EN 301 549 V3.2.1 corresponds to WCAG 2.1. Success criteria that exist only in WCAG 2.2 (2.4.11, 2.5.7, 2.5.8, 3.2.6, 3.3.7, 3.3.8) have no clause there and are shown as "WCAG 2.2 only". Surjection maintains the mapping: when the standard changes it is updated in a Pro release, and every report names the mapping version (MAPPING.version, currently 2026.10) so a report can be traced to the mapping it used.

PDF output uses Playwright with Chromium:
npm i -D playwright npx playwright install chromium

const html = renderReport({ results, branding, client: { name: "Muster AG" }, locale: "de", checklist, history, }); const pdf = await renderPdf(html, { footer: "Pixel & Co" });

Surjection 2 reads files of version 1 and treats them like version 2 (the ids are computed on reading), so --compare-with and baselines from 1.x keep working. Other programs, including Surjection Pro before 1.0.1, need version 2 support or a converted file:

convert recognises results and baselines by their content. It fails with a clear message for files of a newer version than it knows.

Surjection follows semantic versioning. Within a major version nothing listed below is removed or changes its meaning. Breaking changes wait for the next major version and come with a migration guide; the one for 2.0 is Migrating to 2.0.

The fields of surjection.config.json, as described in the config reference and in the JSON schema. What can change in any release

Anything that is exported but not documented, for example helper functions. Which problems the checks find. axe-core is updated regularly and finds more, so a new minor version can report issues on a site that was clean before. Use a baseline and pin the version in CI if you need identical results. Texts of reports, statements and the checklist, including translations. The look of reports, badges and dashboards. Heuristics of our own checks, for example the 200 px threshold of the focus order, if a better rule is found. Such changes are noted in the changelog.

The Pro packages surjection-report, surjection-history and surjection-checklist are released together with the same version numbers and follow the same rules. They read the results file of any compatible free version.

Bugs are fixed in the latest minor version of the current major version. Version 1.x gets security and bug fixes for 12 months after the release of 2.0.0, then it ends.
Automated tests find only part of all barriers. A passing run is no proof of conformance.

Self-hosted webhooks for Node.js and TypeScript: Standard Webhooks signatures, retries, a delivery log and SSRF protection, in your own PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite.
Sooner or later every SaaS product has to send webhooks to its customers. Doing it properly means signing every request, retrying for hours with backoff when a receiver is down, keeping a log your support team can read, refusing URLs that point into your own network and rotating secrets without downtime. Hosted services such as Svix or Hookdeck do this for you, from several hundred dollars a month, and every event and customer URL passes through their infrastructure.
Vector is the same building block as a library. It signs with the Standard Webhooks format that Svix uses, so receivers can verify with any Standard Webhooks or Svix library, retries eight times over about 27 hours, logs every message, delivery and attempt, and keeps all of it in your own PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite. It has no dependencies and runs on Node.js, Bun, Deno and in serverless functions.

Vector Pro adds an embeddable portal for your customers, a typed event catalog, operations tooling and verified inbound webhooks from Stripe, GitHub and others, messages in the format of Slack, Teams, Discord and Google Chat, and OpenTelemetry output. It is installed from a private GitHub Packages registry, licensed per person, with no licence key and no phone-home.

No. Vector is a library that runs inside your own application and keeps its data in your own database. There is no account, no API key and nothing that phones home; events and your customers' URLs never leave your infrastructure.
Can my customers verify the webhooks with Svix or Standard Webhooks libraries?

Yes. Vector signs exactly as the Standard Webhooks specification describes, which is the format Svix uses, so receivers can use the standardwebhooks or svix packages in any language. Vector's own verify() also accepts svix-* headers, and with envelope: false the payload is sent as the whole body, as Svix does.
Can Vector send to Slack, Teams or Discord?

Yes, with Vector Pro. These services do not accept the usual webhook body, so vector-transform writes the message each one expects (Slack blocks, Teams Adaptive Cards, Discord embeds, Google Chat cards) from templates per event type, detects the service from the endpoint URL and escapes event data so it cannot ping @channel or @everyone. The free library has the transform hook it plugs into, so you can also write your own formatter.

Webhooks are delivered at least once, so a retry can arrive twice and, by default, after a later event. Every retry of a message carries the same webhook-id, so receivers should store the ids they have processed and skip repeats. Where order matters, send related events with the same orderingKey (Vector 2.0): for each endpoint and key, the next message is delivered only after the earlier ones succeeded, failed for good or were cancelled. A message that keeps failing therefore delays later messages of the same key, but not other keys. Idempotency keys keep a message from being created twice on the sending side.

An in-memory store for tests and prototypes, a PostgreSQL store that works with pg, postgres.js, Neon, Supabase and PGlite, a MySQL 8 store (mysql2) and a SQLite store (node:sqlite or better-sqlite3). All are safe with several workers. For any other database you implement the VectorStore interface, about fifteen small methods.
Does it work on serverless platforms?

Yes. Instead of the long-running worker you call process() from a cron job, for example a Vercel cron route every minute, and send with deliverNow: true so the first attempt does not wait for the next run. Retries are picked up by the following cron runs.
Can I send webhooks from a fixed IP address?

Yes. Run an egress proxy with a static IP and pass an undici dispatcher such as ProxyAgent to Vector's dispatcher option; on Node.js 24 and later NODEUSEENVPROXY=1 with HTTPSPROXY works without code. Vector still checks the host name against private networks before each request.
Can I use Vector if my application is not written in Node.js?

Yes, with Vector Pro 2.1. The standalone server runs Vector as its own service. Your PHP, Python, Go or Ruby application sends events to its REST API with a plain HTTP request, and the server signs, delivers and retries them from your own PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite database. It includes an admin page and metrics, and comes as an npm package and a Docker image. The free library stays the better fit when your application is already Node.js.

pnpm add @sweberdev/vector
Vector needs Node.js 22 or newer for sending. Verifying also works in browsers, edge runtimes, Bun and Deno.

npx @sweberdev/vector secret
Command | What it does
